The first: al-Tur is a well-known mountain on which God, exalted is He, spoke to Musa, upon him be peace.

The second: It is the mountain of which God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and Mount Sinin﴾ [al-Tin: 2].

One: the Book of Musa, upon him be peace.

Two: the Book that is in the heaven.

Three: the scrolls of the deeds of creation.

The first: It is a house in the highest heaven, near the Throne, and it is described as frequented because of the large number of angels circumambulating it.

The second: It is the Sacred House of God, which is frequented by pilgrims who circumambulate it and who remain in devotion there (al-'akifin).

One: The three places, namely the Mount, the frequented House, and the swelling sea, are places that were for three prophets, in which they would be alone for intimacy with their Lord and for freedom from creation and for address with God. As for the Mount, Musa, upon him be peace, went to it. As for the House, it was Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the swelling sea, it was Yunus, upon him be peace. All of them addressed God there. As for Muhammad (ﷺ), he said: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God," and "I cannot count the praise upon You; You are as You have praised Yourself." As for Yunus, he said: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. Thus these places became noble for these reasons, so God swore by them. He made clear that seeking refuge in them does not benefit against the command of God, exalted is He, as the son of Nuh, upon him be peace, said: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.' One says: "I saw the amir and I entered upon the vizier." When the amir reaches such fame that there is no risk of ambiguity because of his renown, and the describer wants to describe him with greatness, he says: "Today I saw an amir who has no equal, sitting, and upon him are the marks of kings," and you mean that known amir. The reason is that by indefiniteness you indicate that he has gone beyond being known and recognized in the reality of his greatness. Likewise here, al-Tur is not so famous that ambiguity is avoided when it is indefinite, and likewise the frequented House. As for the Noble Book, it is distinguished from all other books, such that the word "Book" does not come to the minds of the hearers from the Prophet (ﷺ) except for that one. Therefore, when ambiguity is avoided and the benefit of definiteness is attained, whether it is mentioned with the article or not, it is for the sake of another benefit, namely the benefit of indefiniteness in mention. Likewise, the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) is well known.

This is because a folded book is not known for what is in it, so He said it is ﴿on parchment unrolled﴾, unlike folded books. According to this meaning, which is the Preserved Tablet, its meaning is: it is unrolled for you, and no one prevents you from reading it. And ﴿on parchment unrolled﴾ is to describe its attribute, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿a Book he will encounter unrolled﴾ [al-Isra': 13]. That is because what is not known, when it is described, is closer in resemblance to being known.

**The fifth issue:** In some surahs He swore by plural things, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the scattering winds﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 1], and His saying: ﴿By those sent forth﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1], and His saying: ﴿By those who pull out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1]. In others He used the singular, as in this surah, where He said: ﴿By the Mount﴾ and did not say "by the mountains" or "by the seas," especially if we say that what is meant by al-Tur is the great mountain, like al-tawd, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We raised above them the Mount﴾ [al-Nisa': 154], that is, the mountain. So what is the wisdom in this? We say: In most of the plural oaths He swore by things in motion, and a single wind is not fixed and enduring so that an oath could be sworn by it. Rather, it is changing in its individuals and enduring in its kinds, and the purpose from it is not attained except through change and alteration. So He said: ﴿By the scattering winds﴾, pointing to the enduring type rather than to a specific, stable individual. As for the mountain, it is fixed and changes little, and any one mountain endures for ages and eons. So He swore by the singular in that case. Likewise His saying: ﴿By the star﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. The wind is not known to be sworn by, whereas al-Tur is known.

What the philosophers say, you have known its weakness many times. His words, exalted is He, ﴿*wa tasiru al-jibalu sayra*﴾ ("and the mountains will be set moving"), indicate the contrary of their view. This is because they agreed that the departure of a great mountain from its place is possible. How could it not be, when they themselves say that the quaking of the earth, together with the mountains in it, is caused by vapour gathering beneath the earth which shakes it? If that is so, we say: the sky is capable of motion by taking it out of its natural directions, while the mountain is still and its nature requires stillness. If one body accepts motion even though it is contrary to its nature, then another body accepting it, being in agreement with its nature, is more appropriate. Their saying that what accepts circular motion does not accept linear motion is extremely weak. His words ﴿*mawran*﴾ ("a shaking") convey a noble benefit, namely that His words ﴿*wa tasiru al-jibal*﴾ may be an explanation of how the sky shakes. This is because when the mountains move and carry their inhabitants with them, it appears that the sky is like a moving thing in the opposite direction, as the passenger of a ship observes, for he sees a still mountain as moving. So someone could say: "The sky shakes in appearance (*ra'y al-'ayn*) because of the motion of the mountains, just as the passenger of a ship sees the moon as moving. If the sky shakes in this way, then there is no escape or refuge, neither in the sky nor in the earth."

As for the wisdom, it is the announcement and notification that there is no return to this world. This is because the earth, the mountains, the sky and the stars are all for the cultivation of this world and for the benefit of the children of Adam from them. If there is no return for them, there is no benefit in them, so God, exalted is He, annihilates them.

Although they disagreed with us in both issues, and the philosophers agreed with us in one of them but not the other, yet they followed the path of illusion and did not hold themselves to the path of consistency regarding times.

If it is said: "Then what is before the first renewing thing?" We say: nothing is before it. If it is said: "Is its non-existence before it, or is its non-existence before it?" So it is with what we have said.

If it is said: "This is not valid, because God, exalted is He, is an existing thing, and He is before the world," we say: our statement "there is nothing before the first renewing thing" means "there is nothing before it in time." As for God, exalted is He, He is not before it in time, since God was and there was no time, and time came into existence together with the first renewing thing.

If it is said: "Then what is the meaning of God's existence before every thing other than Him?" We say: its meaning is that God was and there was nothing other than Him. It is not said: "What you mentioned is establishing a thing by a thing, and that thing is not established except by what you intend to establish, for the beginning of time is your aim, and it is based on the first renewing thing, and the dispute concerns renewal." This is because for the opponent there is no first renewing thing in existence, but rather before every renewing thing. We say: we did not mention that as a proof, but we mentioned it to show that there is no compulsion (*ilzam*) upon us, and that nothing is directed at us if we say that the world is originated (*hudus*), the dimensions are finite, and there is necessity and compulsion. Thus the first statement stands, and then he compels us and says: "Do you not say that for us there is a first renewing thing? So say similarly to him that there is a non-existence." We then say: "No, rather there is nothing before it in time," so this is a general negation, and it is only because time is absent, as we mentioned in the example.

When you know this, time becomes at one time existing together with an accident, and at another time existing after an accident. This is because our present day and the other days are all distinguished by the first renewing thing, and the first renewing thing has a time with which it is. When you know that the matters of time and place are obscure to some understandings, and the hidden matter is known through description and attribution: if you say "a boy" it is not known, but if you describe him or attribute him and say "a small boy" or "a big boy," or "a white one" or "a black one," it comes close to understanding. Likewise, if you say "the boy of Zayd," it comes closer, and there is no escape from knowing the time. A thing is not known except by what is specific to it. When you say of a human "a living being that exists," you put him far from understanding, and when you say "a living being of tall stature," you bring him close to it. So in the case of time, it must be known by what is specific to it, because the past verb, the future verb and the present verb are specific to times, and the verbal noun has an unrestricted time. If you say "the time of the going out," it is distinguished from the time of entering and others. When you say "the day when Fulan went out," it conveys what "the day of the going out" conveys, with an addition, namely that it is distinguished from "the day when Fulan goes out." Attribution to what is more distinguishing is better. Just as when you say "the boy of a man," you distinguish him from "the boy of a woman," and when you say "the boy of Zayd," you add to the meaning and it is better, so our saying "the day when he went out" is better for identifying that day than your saying "the day of the going out." From this discussion it is clear that time is connected to the verb, and other things are not connected to it, because the verb is specific to time and not to other things. The exception is place in the phrase "sit where he sits," since *haythu* is connected to clauses because of the resemblance of the adverb of place to the adverb of time. As for clauses, they are only valid through the mediation of their containing a verb. So one does not say "*yawma Zaydun akhuka*" ("on the day Zayd is your brother"), but one says "*yawma Zaydun fihi kharij*" ("on the day Zayd is going out in it").

Among the verbal benefits is that *lata* (not) is specific in its usage to time. God, exalted is He, said ﴿*wa la-ta hina manas*﴾ ("and there was no time for escape") [Sad: 3]. One does not say *lata al-rajulu su'*. This is because time is renewal after renewal, and life does not remain after death for another life, and after every movement there is another movement, and after every time there is another time. To this His words point, exalted is He: ﴿*kulla yawmin huwa fi sha'n*﴾ ("Every day He is in a matter") [al-Rahman: 29], meaning: before creation He had not created anything, but after He created, He is forever continually creating one thing after another. So after our life there is death, after our death there is life, after our life there is reckoning, and after the reckoning there is a lasting reward or a lasting punishment, which is necessary, and God does not abandon the act. Since time is far from negation, extra letters were added to the negating particles. If it is said: "God, exalted is He, is further from non-existence, so *ta'* should not be brought close to *la* there," we say: ﴿*wa la-ta hina manas*﴾ [Sad: 3] is an interpretation (*ta'wil*), and according to it what you mentioned does not arise, namely that *la* is the one assimilated to *laysa* (is not). Its estimated meaning is "the time is not a time of escape," and this is the well-known view. For this reason it is specific to *hin* (time) rather than to day and night, because *hin* is more lasting than night and day: night and day may not be, while *hin* is.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So woe on that day to the deniers, those who are playing in their idle talk.﴾

Meaning: when it is known that the punishment of God is certain to occur and that there is no one who can repel it, then "woe" is due to the deniers. The *fa'* (فَ, "so", the particle of consequence) indicates the connection of meaning. It signals the assurance of safety for the people of faith. This is because when He said, ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is bound to occur﴾, He did not specify on whom it would fall. So when He said, ﴿So woe on that day to the deniers﴾, the one to whom it is specifically directed became known, namely the denier. There are several issues here:

**The first issue:** If you say that His statement ﴿So woe on that day to the deniers﴾ explains who is struck by the punishment and upon whom it descends, then whoever does not deny is not punished. Thus the people of major sins will not be punished, because they do not deny. We say: that punishment does not fall upon the people of major sins. This is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Every time a company is thrown into it, its keepers will ask them, "Did no warner come to you?" They will say, "Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied him."﴾ [al-Mulk: 8–9]. So we say that the believer is not cast into it with humiliation; rather, he enters it so that he may be purified, with a kind of honoring. Likewise, "woe" is for the deniers.

"Woe" (al-waylu, الوَيْلُ) indicates severity, and the combination of the letters *wāw*, *yā'* and *lām* never separates from a kind of severity. From it comes *lawā* (لَوى), meaning "he pushed away," and *lawā yalwī* (لَوى يَلْوِي), meaning "he was strong." *Al-waliyy* (الوَلِيُّ) in this root carries the sense of strength over the one under one's charge. This is indicated by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿the day they will be thrust violently into the fire﴾ (*yudaʿʿūna*, يُدَعُّونَ), for the denier is thrust, while the one who affirms is not thrust.

We have already mentioned the permissibility of indefiniteness (*tankīr*, التَّنْكِيرُ) in His statement *wayl* (ويْلٌ), despite it being the subject (*mubtada'*, مُبْتَدَأٌ), because it is in the sense of an accusative, since it is a supplication (*duʿāʾ*). Its justification has already been given in His statement: ﴿He said, "Peace"﴾ [Maryam: 47].

As for *al-khawḍ* (الخَوْضُ) itself, in the Qur'anic usage it is specific to plunging into falsehoods. This is why He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and you plunged in as those before you plunged﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69], and He said: ﴿and we used to plunge with those who plunged﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 45].

The indefiniteness of *khawḍ* (الخَوْضِ) allows two possibilities:

First: it may be for intensification, meaning "in a complete, great plunging."

Second: the nunation (*tanwīn*, التَّنْوِينُ) may be a substitute (*taʿwīḍ*) for the omitted *mudāf ilayh* (مُضافٌ إليه, the genitive complement), as in His statement, exalted is He: (*illā*, إلًّا) [al-Tawbah: 8], and His statement ﴿and each﴾ [al-Furqan: 39], and ﴿some of them against others﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. The original form of "their plunging" is "the known plunging of theirs."

His statement ﴿those who are in plunging﴾ is not a descriptive qualifier (*waṣf*) of the deniers that distinguishes them from others. Rather, it is for censure (*dhamm*), just as you say "the accursed Satan" (*al-shayṭān al-rajīm*) without intending to separate him from a Satan who is not accursed. This is unlike your saying "honor the learned man," where the qualifier distinguishes him. So the description "accursed" is for censure, not for definition. And you say in praise: "God, who created," and "God, the Mighty," for praise, not to distinguish Him from a god who did not create or from a god who is not mighty, since God is one, without any other.

Then He, exalted is He, said: "On the Day they will be thrust into the fire of Hell with a violent thrust."

There are linguistic and semantic discussions concerning this. As for the linguistic ones, there are several issues:

The first issue: "Yawma" (on the day) is governed by what? We say the apparent view is that it is governed by what follows it, which is indicated by His saying: "This is the Fire" [al-Tur: 14]. Its implied meaning is: "On the day they are thrust, it will be said to them: This is the Fire which you used to deny." It is also possible to read otherwise: that "yawma" is a substitute (badal) for "yawma" in "yawma'idhin," so that the sense is: "Woe on that day to the deniers," and "on the day they are thrust," i.e., the deniers. This is because His saying "yawma'idhin" [al-Tur: 11] means "on the day the punishment befalls," and that day is "the day they are thrust" into the Fire.

The second issue: His saying "they are thrust into the Fire" indicates the terror of the Fire of Hell, because its guardians do not approach it; rather they push its inhabitants towards it from a distance and cast them into it while they themselves do not draw near to it.

The third issue: "Da'ًّan" (with a violent thrust) is a verbal noun (masdar). I have already mentioned the benefit of mentioning verbal nouns, which is to indicate that the thrusting is a real, recognised thrust, of which it is said that it is a thrust and not that it is "not a thrust," just as a speaker says of a light blow, belittling it: "This is not a blow," and of a contemptible enemy: "This is not an enemy," and of a base man: "He is not a man." This holds in the case of verbal nouns, except according to the reading of one who reads "yud'awna ila nari jahannama du'a'" (they are called to the Fire of Hell with a calling), for then "du'a'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), its implied meaning being: "It will be said to them: 'Come to the Fire,' being summoned to it."

As for the semantic aspects, we say: His saying "on the day they are thrust into the Fire of Hell" indicates that its guardians cast them into it while they are far from it. And He, exalted is He, said: "On the day they are dragged into the Fire" [al-Qamar: 48]. We say the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: the angels drag them within the Fire, then when they approach a specific fire, which is the Fire of Hell, they cast them into it from a distance; so the dragging is within the Fire, and the thrusting is into a fire that is more intense and more powerful. This is indicated by His saying: "They will be dragged [in the boiling water], then in the Fire they will be kindled" [Ghafir: 71–72], meaning that they will have dragging in the heat of the Fire, and after that they will have being made to enter it.

The second: it is permissible that at every time there are angels in charge of them: to the Fire one angel pushes them, and within the Fire another drags them.

The third: it is permissible that the dragging is with chains, so that they are dragged within the Fire while the one dragging is outside the Fire.

The fourth: it is possible that the angels thrust the people of the Fire into the Fire as humiliation and contempt for them, then they enter the Fire with them and drag them within it.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is this magic, or is it that you do not see?﴾ This is for the sake of confirming the matter. The reason is that whoever sees something while the matter is not as he sees it, that error must be due to one of two things: either something related to the thing seen, or something related to the one who sees. So His words ﴿Is this magic?﴾ mean: Is there doubt in what is seen, or is there a defect in your sight? This is a rhetorical question of denial (istifham inkar), meaning that neither of the two is established. What you see is true, although you used to say that it is not true. He said ﴿Is this magic?﴾ because they used to attribute the things they saw to magic. They would say that the splitting of the moon and similar things were magic. On that day, when pain perceived by the sense of touch came upon them together with sight, and the torment reached its utmost limit, they could no longer say, "This is magic." Otherwise, it would not have been valid for them to ask to be freed from the Fire.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Burn therein; so be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ That is: since you cannot deny it, and it is confirmed that it is not magic nor a defect in your sight, then burn in it. His words ﴿So be patient or be not patient﴾ contain two benefits. The first is to show that there is no escape and no refuge. Whoever does not endure pushes the thing away from himself, either by repelling the one who torments him, thereby preventing him, or by angering him so that he kills him and gives him rest. None of this benefits in the torment of the Hereafter. Whoever cannot overcome the tormentor so as to repel him, and cannot be freed by annihilation, will not be decreed to die. Thus patience is like its absence, because whoever is patient remains in it, and whoever is not patient remains in it. The second benefit is to show what distinguishes the torment of the Hereafter from the torment of this world. The one tormented in this world, if he is patient, may benefit from his patience, either by reward in the Hereafter or by praise in this world, so it is said of him, "How brave he is, and how strong his heart!" If he panics, he is blamed, and it is said, "He panics like children and women." But in the Hereafter there is no praise and no reward for patience. His words ﴿It is the same for you﴾: "sawa'" (equal, the same) is the predicate, and its subject is implied by His words ﴿So be patient or be not patient﴾. It is as if He says: patience and its absence are the same. If it is said that this entails an increase in torment, and that it entails punishment for an intention that was not carried out, we say that there is a subtle point in this. The believer, through his faith, learns that the good he intends is rewarded, and that the evil he intends but does not carry out is not punished. The disbeliever, through his disbelief, has become the opposite: the good he intends but does not do is not rewarded, and the evil he intends and which actually happens from him is punished, and there is no injustice in that. God, exalted is He, informed him of this, and he chose it and entered into it by his own choice. It is as if God, exalted is He, said: whoever disbelieves and dies as a disbeliever, I shall torment him forever, so beware. And whoever believes, I shall reward him forever. Thus whoever commits disbelief and persists in it after hearing this, when the punisher punishes him forever, in fulfilment of what He threatened him with, he is not unjust.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 52, verse 21:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who believed, and whose offspring followed them in faith, We shall join their offspring with them﴾. There are in this several subtle points (lata'if, singular latifah).

The first: the compassion of fatherhood, as it is in this world, is complete, and likewise in the Hereafter. For this reason God, exalted is He, comforts the hearts of His servants by telling them that He will not separate them from their children but will gather them together. If it is said: you have mentioned in the explanation of some verses that God consoles fathers for their children and the reverse, and that the father who is among the people of Paradise does not remember the son who is among the people of Hellfire. We say: the young child found in his father good fatherhood, and no opposition to it was found. For this reason God joins the child to the parent in Islam in the world, while young, and when he grows up he becomes independent. If he disbelieves, he is attributed to someone other than his father. This is because Islam, for Muslims, is like a father. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The believers are only brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10]. The plural of akh (brother) is used in the sense of brotherhood by birth, and ikhwan (brothers) is its plural used in the sense of brotherhood of friendship and love. Therefore, disbelief in terms of sense and custom is a father; if he opposes his father's religion, he becomes, in terms of the Shari'ah, another father. In this is guidance for fathers that nothing should distract them from compassion toward the child. It is therefore a foul and gross thing for a person to busy himself with strolling in the garden with beloved brothers instead of providing sustenance for the children. How could the people of Paradise not be occupied, with what is in Paradise of the wide-eyed houris, from their children, until they remember them? So God comforted their hearts by His saying ﴿We shall join their offspring with them﴾. If this is so, then what is your opinion of the sinner who squanders his wealth on what is forbidden and leaves his children begging from the faces of the base and the noble? We seek refuge in God from him. This indicates that whoever bequeaths lawful wealth to his children, a charity is written for him by it. For this reason it is not permitted for the sick person to dispose of more than a third (of his estate).

The second subtle point: God's saying ﴿and whose offspring followed them﴾. This should be evidence that in the Hereafter we will be joined to them, because in the abode of this world the observance of causes is greater. For this reason God has not made it His custom to send food down from heaven before a person; what is obtained for him through planting, grinding and kneading, he eats. In the Hereafter He gives him that without effort, as a reward for what he strove for before. Therefore this should be taken as clear evidence that God joins to him his child, even if the child has not done righteous deeds, just as the child followed him, even if the child has not witnessed or believed anything.

The third subtle point: in God's saying ﴿in faith﴾. God made the child follow the parents in faith, and did not make him follow his father in disbelief. The proof is that whoever among the disbelievers embraces Islam, his children are judged to be Muslims. Whoever among the Muslims apostatizes, God forbid, his child is not judged to be a disbeliever.

The fourth subtle point: in this world He said ﴿and We made them follow﴾ [al-Qasas: 42], and in the Hereafter He said ﴿We shall join them﴾. This is because in this world the young follower cannot attain equality with the one followed, and he is only a follower while the father is the origin, due to the superiority of the one who strives over the one who does not strive. But in the Hereafter, when God joins the child to him by His grace, there is given to the child a rank like that of his father.

[Page 216]

The fifth subtle point: in God's saying ﴿and We did not deprive them﴾, there is a consolation for their hearts and removal of the delusion of one who imagines that the reward of the father's deed is divided between the parent and the child. Rather, the parent has the reward of his deed by the grace of striving, and his children have the like of it by God's bounty and mercy.

The sixth subtle point: in God's saying ﴿of their deed﴾, and He did not say ﴿of their reward﴾. This is because God's saying ﴿and We did not deprive them of their deed﴾ is evidence of the continuation of their deed as it was, and the reward is for the deed together with an increase. So in it is an indication of the continuation of the deed to which belongs a great reward, the excess above it, and the magnificent return to it. If He had said ﴿We did not deprive them of their reward﴾, that would have been achieved with the least thing, because whatever God gives His servant for his deed is a complete reward. And because if He had said ﴿We did not deprive them of their reward﴾, it would still have been possible to say that God graciously bestowed on him complete reward for incomplete deed and gave him abundant reward, although his deed was for him and his child together. There are in this questions:

The first question: God's saying ﴿And those who believed﴾ is conjoined to what? We say: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿Indeed the God-fearing﴾.

The second question: if that is so, why did He repeat the phrase ﴿those who believed﴾, when the intended meaning would be achieved by His saying ﴿We shall join their offspring with them﴾ after His saying ﴿and We shall pair them﴾, and the sense would become ﴿and We paired them and joined with them﴾? We say: there is a benefit in it, which is that the God-fearing are those who guarded against shirk and disobedience, and they are ﴿those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ [al-Ra'd: 29]. Here He said ﴿those who believed﴾, meaning that with the existence of faith his child becomes among the people of Paradise. Then if the father commits a major sin or a minor sin persisted in, his child is not punished for it; rather the parent is, and perhaps the son enters Paradise before the father. In this there is a subtle spiritual point, which is that it is reported in the traditions that the young child intercedes for his father, and that is an indication of the reward.

The third question: is anything other than this permissible? We say: yes, it is permissible that God's saying ﴿those who believed﴾ be conjoined to ﴿with houris, wide-eyed﴾; its estimated sense is: We paired them with wide-eyed houris, that is, We joined them with them, and with those who believed. This is an indication of His saying ﴿as brothers, facing one another on couches﴾ [al-Hijr: 47], that is, We gathered their scattered affairs with spouses, brothers and children by His saying ﴿and We made them follow﴾ [al-Qasas: 42]. This is the view mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. But the first is better and more correct. If it is said: how is the report in the past tense correct on this view, when after joining them together He (glorified and exalted is He) ...? We say: the past tense in ﴿and We paired them﴾ is correct according to what God mentioned of their marriage to them by Us from the day He created them, even if the time of union was delayed.

The fourth question: ﴿their offspring﴾ is read in plural in both places, ﴿dhurriyyatihim﴾ in both is read in singular, and in the first it is read ﴿dhurriyyatuhum﴾ and in the second ﴿dhurriyyatahum﴾. Is there a reason for the third reading? We say: yes, a semantic reason, not a verbal one. This is because the believer is followed by his offspring in faith, even if they do not exist, in the sense that if he had a thousand children they would be his followers in faith by judgment. As for joining, it is not by judgment; it is only in fact, and that applies to existing ones. So the followers are more numerous than those joined, therefore the first is in plural and the second in singular.

The fifth question: what is the benefit of the indefiniteness of faith in His saying ﴿and We made their offspring follow them in faith﴾? We say: it is either specification or indefiniteness, as if He were saying: We made their offspring follow them in sincere, complete faith; or He says: We made them follow with some faith, whatever part of it. This is because complete faith is not found in the child, as the proof is that whoever has a young child is judged to be a believer by his faith. When he reaches maturity and openly declares disbelief and denies the following, it is said that he is not an apostate, and it becomes clear by his statement that he did not follow. And it is said that he is an apostate, because he disbelieved after he was judged to be a believer, like the original Muslim. So by this difference it becomes clear that his faith is strengthened. These two aspects al-Zamakhshari mentioned. It may be that the intended meaning is other than this, namely that the tanwin (nunation) is in place of a substitute for the genitive complement, as in His saying ﴿some of them by means of others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 251] and His saying ﴿and to each God promised the best﴾ [al-Nisa': 95]. Its explanation is that the estimated sense is: We made their offspring follow them with faith, that is, by means of their faith, because following is not faith however it is and from whomever it is, but it is the faith of the fathers. However the idafah (genitive construction) indicates a restriction, and that the faith is not faith absolutely. For the saying of one who says "the water of the tree" and "the water of the pomegranate" is correct, but the unqualified name "water" without an idafah is not correct. So His saying ﴿in faith﴾ suggests that it is faith attributed to them, as He said: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85], where He affirmed the attributed faith although it was not faith. He cut off the idafah while intending it, so that it would be known that it is sound faith, and He substituted the tanwin so that it would be known that it does not bring security in this world except the faith of the fathers. This is a good aspect.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾. Al-Wahidi said: this is a return to the mention of the people of the Fire, for they are held in pledge in the Fire, but the believer is not held in pledge. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾ is general for every individual held as a pledge with God through his earning; if he earns good, He releases his neck, and otherwise he is bound by the pledge. What appears from it is that it is general regarding every individual. There is in the verse another aspect, which is that al-rahin (the pledge) is fa'il in the sense of the active participle, so the meaning, and God knows best, is: every person, by what he has earned, is a continuing one (rahin), that is, lasting. If he does good, he is in Paradise forever; if he does evil, he is in the Fire eternally. We have mentioned that in this world the permanence of deeds depends on the permanence of substances, for an accident does not remain except in a substance and is not found except in it. In the Hereafter the permanence of substances depends on the permanence of deeds, for God preserves their deeds, because they are with God among the enduring righteous deeds, and what is with God endures, and the enduring remains with its doer.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾.

That is, We increased them in food and drink. As for food, it is fruit and meat; as for drink, it is the cup they pass to one another (al-ka's alladhi yatanazi'una fiha). In its explanation there are subtle points:

The first subtle point: When He said, ﴿And We joined them with their offspring﴾ [al-Tur: 21], He explained the increase, so that it would follow the custom of kings in this world: when they increase the provision of one of their servants, they increase the allowances of his bread and his fiefs. He chose from among food the highest kinds, which are fruit and meat, for they are the food of those who live in luxury. And He gathered good attributes in His saying "of whatever they desire," because if He had mentioned a particular kind, that kind might not be desired by some people; so He said that everyone is given what he desires. If it is said that desire is like hunger, and there is in it a kind of pain, we say: it is not so. Rather, desire in it is pleasure, and Allah the Exalted does not leave one in desire without the object desired so that he suffers; rather, the object desired is present together with the appetite. And a person in this world only suffers from one of two things: either from genuine desire and his inability to reach the object desired, or from the availability of various kinds of food and drink to him while his appetite has ceased. Both of these are absent in the Hereafter.

The second subtle point: When He said, ﴿nor did We diminish it﴾, the negation of deficiency is satisfied by the attainment of equality, so He said: the absence of deficiency is not by limiting to equality, but by another way, namely increase and augmentation. If it is said: Allah has mentioned eating and drinking much, while some of the knowers say that for those specially devoted to Allah there is a preoccupation that distracts them from eating and drinking and everything other than Allah, we say: this is in regard to action, and for this reason the Exalted said: ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24], and He said: ﴿for what you used to do﴾ [al-Tur: 19]. As for knowledge of this, that is another matter; for this reason He said: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for. Peace, a word from a Lord Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57-58]. That is: for the souls is what they enjoy as fruit, and for the spirits is what they wish for of nearness and closeness.

His saying the Exalted, ﴿they pass to one another a cup﴾, this is according to the custom of kings when they sit in their assemblies for drinking, and fruits and meats are brought to them while they are drinking. His saying the Exalted, ﴿yatanazi'una﴾, means they hand it to one another (yata'atawna). It may be said that tanazu' means mutual pulling, and then their pulling is the pulling of playfulness, not the pulling of contention; and in it there is a kind of pleasure, and it clarifies the state of drink in this world, for they boast of drinking much and do not boast of eating much. For this reason, when one of them drinks, the other considers it necessary to drink the same as his drinking companion drank, and does not consider it necessary to eat the same as his table companion and sitting companion ate.

His saying the Exalted, ﴿There is no idle talk therein, nor any sinfulness﴾. Whether we say that (fiha) refers to Paradise or to the cup, its mention is because the mention of drink and its description as in this world has been mentioned. So He said, the Exalted: In drinking in the Hereafter there is not all that is in it in this world of idle talk, due to loss of reason, nor of sinfulness which arises due to the rising of desire and anger when reason and understanding are at their fullness. And there is a third aspect: that it is said that it does not overtake him as it overtakes the drinker in this world, so he is not sinful, i.e., he is not attributed to sin. And there is a fourth aspect: that the intended meaning of sinfulness (ta'thim) is intoxication, and in that case there is a fine ordering in it. This is because some people become intoxicated and yet have a steady mind and are not accustomed to rowdiness; so they calm down and sleep, and do not harm or get harmed, nor do they rave or listen to one who raves. And among them is one who becomes rowdy. So He said: ﴿There is no idle talk therein.﴾

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there will go round among them young boys of their own, as if they were hidden pearls﴾ — that is, with the cups.

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There will go round among them youths who remain forever young, with goblets and ewers and a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17–18]. His saying "of their own" (lahum) means "belonging to them" (milkuhum), informing them of their power to dispose of these youths by command, prohibition and service. This is the well-known view, but it admits of another aspect: when He, exalted is He, clarified the distinction of the wine of the Hereafter from the wine of this world, He clarified the distinction of the youths of the Hereafter from the youths of this world. For in this world, when youths go round among masters and kings, they go round among them for their own benefit, either out of expectation of gain or to secure pardon. In the Hereafter, however, their going round among the people of Paradise is purely for the sake of those people and their benefit, and they have no need of them. A youth whose condition is this has a distinction over others, and he may even reach the rank of children.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as if they were pearls﴾: that is, in purity. And ﴿hidden﴾ is to convey an increase in the purity of their complexions, or to explain that they are like sheltered ones who do not come out or go forth from their presence, so they remain within their protection.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning each other. They will say: "Before this, we were fearful among our people. But God has been gracious to us and has protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind. Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Most Kind, the Most Merciful."﴾ This is an indication that they know what befell them in the world and remember it. Likewise the disbeliever does not forget the bounties he had in the world, so the believer's delight increases from the viewpoint that he sees himself moved from prison to Paradise and from constraint to spaciousness, while the disbeliever's pain increases as he sees himself moved from honour to ruin and from bliss to the Blazing Fire. Then they recall what they used to be in the world of fear and dread, and so they say ﴿Before this, we were fearful among our people﴾. Their questioning concerns the cause of what they have reached, so they say: "The fear of God—we used to fear God." ﴿But God has been gracious to us and has protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind.﴾ In this there is a subtle point, namely that their fear may have been over the loss of the world, leaving it, and parting from their companions. Then, when they entered Paradise, they realised their error.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Or do their minds command them to this, or are they a transgressing people?﴾ This *am* (أمْ), too, as we have mentioned, is connected, and its implied sense is: "Has a revelation (ذِكْر) been sent down to them? Or do their minds (aḥlāmuhum) command them to this?" That is because things are established either by transmitted evidence (samʿ) or by reason (ʿaql). So He said: Has a transmitted command come down? Or do their intellects command them to what they say? Or are they a transgressing people who are deceived and say what has no transmitted evidence and no rational basis? *Al-ṭughyān* (transgression) is exceeding the limit in disobedience, and likewise everything whose outward appearance is disliked. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose beyond its bounds﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:11]. There are several issues here:

**The First Issue:** If the intended meaning is what you mentioned, why was what precedes it omitted? We say: That what they say is ascribed to a transmitted report, whose absence is known, does not negate it. As for it being rational, they used to claim that it was rational. As for their being transgressors, that is true. So God specified by mention what they said and what God said about it. They said, "We follow reason," while God said, "They are transgressors." Thus He mentioned the two matters over which disagreement occurred.

**The Second Issue:** His saying ﴿Their minds (aḥlāmuhum) command them﴾ indicates that whatever does not conform to reason should not be said; rather, one should say only what reason requires being said. So has every obligation of reason become something commanded?

**The Third Issue:** What are *al-aḥlām*? We say: it is the plural of *ḥilm*, which means intellect (ʿaql). The two are of one category in meaning, because intellect restrains a person, so he is like a tethered camel that does not move from its place. *Ḥilm* also comes from *al-ḥilm* (forbearance), which is likewise the cause of a person's dignity and steadiness. Similarly, intellects are called *al-nuhā*, from *al-nahy* (prohibition), which means restraint. There is a subtle point here: in the basic linguistic sense, *ḥilm* is what a sleeper sees, whereupon he ejaculates and must perform ghusl; it is the cause of puberty, and with it a person becomes accountable. It seems that God, in His subtle wisdom, joined desire to intellect, and when desire appears, intellect is complete. So He pointed to intellect by pointing to what accompanies it, which is *ḥilm*, so that one would know that it is a sign of the completeness of intellect, not the intellect by which a person guards against shirk and entry into the Fire. On this basis, there is an emphasis on what we mentioned: a person should not say everything that is rational; rather, he should say only what sound, grave intellect commands, which validates accountability.

**The Fourth Issue:** To what does *hādhā* (this) refer? We say there are several views:

First: It refers to the matter that appears from them in word and deed, where they worship idols and images and utter nonsensical speech.

Second: It refers to their saying, "He is a soothsayer, he is a poet, he is a madman."

Third: It refers to waiting (*al-tarabbuṣ*). When they said, "We await," God the Exalted said, "Do their intellects command them to await their own destruction?" For no one who anticipated the destruction of his prophet failed to be destroyed.

**The Fifth Issue:** Can *am* (أمْ) in this place mean *bal* (بَلْ, "rather")? We say yes. Its implied sense is: They say, "He is a poet," verbally; rather, they believe it by reason, and it enters their minds. That is, this is not something they say without reason; rather, they believe him to be a soothsayer and a madman. This is indicated by the reading of one who recited *bal hum qawmun ṭāghūn* (﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people﴾). However, *bal* is clear here, while in His saying *bal tamurruhum aḥlāmuhum* it is hidden.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Rather, they do not believe﴾. It is connected to His saying, ﴿Or do they say, "A poet, for whom we await misfortune"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30]. Its implied meaning, according to what we have mentioned, is: "Do you say he is a soothsayer, or do you say he is a poet, or do you say he has invented it?"

Then, to refute all the categories, He said: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful﴾. That is: if he is a poet, then among you are eloquent poets and clever soothsayers, and those who extemporize speeches and qasidas and recount tales, whose additions and omissions do not differ. So let them produce something like what he produced. The verb taqawwala is used to mean lying. There is also in this a subtle indication: the form tafa''ala (taf'ul) denotes feigning and displaying something that is not as it appears. It is said: "So-and-so pretended to be ill (tamarrada)," meaning he was not ill, but displayed illness from himself. In that case, it is as if they were saying, "It is a lie, and not a (true) saying; it is merely the feigning of the appearance of speech, and in reality it is not speech at all," so that it is known that the one who denies is the truthful one. His saying, ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾, explains this: at the time the revelation descended and the miracle occurred, they were witnessing it, and this should have required that they bear witness on his behalf before others and be like the stars for the believers, as the Companions (may God be pleased with them) were. Yet they were not like that, but even less than that: they were not even among the ordinary believers who had not witnessed those events, and the matter did not become manifest to them with that clarity.

His saying, ﴿So let them produce﴾: the fa' indicates sequence (ta'qib), meaning: if it is so, then it is obligatory upon them to produce something like what he produced, in order to validate their speech and invalidate his. Regarding this there are several discussions:

The first: Some scholars said: ﴿So let them produce﴾ is a command of incapacitation (amr ta'jiz), like one's saying to someone who claims a matter or an act, intending to show his incapacity. The apparent view is that the command here remains on its literal meaning, because He did not say "produce" absolutely, but said "produce, if you are truthful." On this supposition, and given the existence of that condition, it is obligatory to produce it. The command of incapacitation in God's speech is His saying: ﴿Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west,﴾ so the one who disbelieved was confounded [al-Baqarah: 258]. This is not a discussion that causes any defect in their speech.

The second: The Mu'tazilah said: "discourse (hadith) is originated (muhdath), and the Qur'an called it discourse, so it is originated." We say: hadith is a homonymous term (ism mushtarak); it is applied to the originated and to the eternal. For this reason, it is valid to say "this is an ancient discourse" in the sense of something long past in time, not in the sense of negating priority; and there is no dispute about that.

The third: The grammarians say: the adjective follows the modified noun in definiteness and indefiniteness, but the modified noun here is "hadith," which is indefinite, while "mithl" is construed with "the Qur'an," and what is construed with a definite noun is definite. How is this? We say: mithl and ghayr do not become definite through annexation, and likewise everything that is like them. The reason is that ghayr, mithl, and their like are in the extreme of indefiniteness. When you say "I have not seen anything like Zayd," it encompasses everything, for every thing is like Zayd in being a thing; the inanimate is like him in body, bulk and possibility; the plant is like him in growth, increase, withering and perishing; the animal is like him in motion, perception and other attributes. As for ghayr, when annexed it is made indefinite, and when the annexation is cut off it may become definite; for when you say "ghayr Zayd" it becomes in extreme vagueness, since it encompasses countless things. But when you detach it from annexation, you may say "al-ghayr" and "al-mughayarah" are of one category, and likewise "al-taghayyur," so you make ghayr like the names of genera, or you make it a subject (mubtada') and intend by it a specific meaning.

The fourth: ﴿If they are truthful﴾ means in their saying ﴿He has invented it﴾ [al-Tur: 33]. We have mentioned that this refers back to what preceded: that he is a soothsayer, that he is a madman, that he is a poet, that he is an inventor. Had they been truthful in any of these, producing the like of the Qur'an would have been easy for them; and since they were unable, they lied in all of it.

The fifth discussion: We have mentioned that the Qur'an is miraculous, and there is no doubt about it, for the creatures were unable, when challenged, to produce anything close to it. Its being miraculous is either because of its eloquence, which is the view of the majority of the People of the Sunnah; or because God diverted the intellects of the intelligent from producing its like, and bound their tongues from uttering anything close to it, and prevented the capable from doing what is within their power—like one who performs an act no one else can do. For if someone says to another, "I will move this mountain," it is considered far-fetched from him; and likewise if he says, "I will do an act with which the creatures cannot lift an apple from its place," it is considered far-fetched from him. Each of these, when joined to the claim, is a miraculous act. This is the view of some theologians, and there is no flaw in it; and it may also be said that it is miraculous by both together.

In that case, it is as if they were saying, "It is a lie, and not a (true) saying; it is merely the feigning of the appearance of speech, and in reality it is not speech at all," so that it is known that the one who denies is the truthful one. His saying, ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾, explains this: at the time the revelation descended and the miracle occurred, they were witnessing it, and this should have required that they bear witness on his behalf before others and be like the stars for the believers, as the Companions (may God be pleased with them) were. Yet they were not like that, but even less than that: they were not even among the ordinary believers who had not witnessed those events, and the matter did not become manifest to them with that clarity.

His saying, ﴿So let them produce﴾: the fa' indicates sequence (ta'qib), meaning: if it is so, then it is obligatory upon them to produce something like what he produced, in order to validate their speech and invalidate his. Regarding this there are several discussions:

The first: Some scholars said: ﴿So let them produce﴾ is a command of incapacitation (amr ta'jiz), like one's saying to someone who claims a matter or an act, intending to show his incapacity. The apparent view is that the command here remains on its literal meaning, because He did not say "produce" absolutely, but said "produce, if you are truthful." On this supposition, and given the existence of that condition, it is obligatory to produce it. The command of incapacitation in God's speech is His saying: ﴿Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west,﴾ so the one who disbelieved was confounded [al-Baqarah: 258]. This is not a discussion that causes any defect in their speech.

The second: The Mu'tazilah said: "discourse (hadith) is originated (muhdath), and the Qur'an called it discourse, so it is originated." We say: hadith is a homonymous term (ism mushtarak); it is applied to the originated and to the eternal. For this reason, it is valid to say "this is an ancient discourse" in the sense of something long past in time, not in the sense of negating priority; and there is no dispute about that.

The third: The grammarians say: the adjective follows the modified noun in definiteness and indefiniteness, but the modified noun here is "hadith," which is indefinite, while "mithl" is construed with "the Qur'an," and what is construed with a definite noun is definite. How is this? We say: mithl and ghayr do not become definite through annexation, and likewise everything that is like them. The reason is that ghayr, mithl, and their like are in the extreme of indefiniteness. When you say "I have not seen anything like Zayd," it encompasses everything, for every thing is like Zayd in being a thing; the inanimate is like him in body, bulk and possibility; the plant is like him in growth, increase, withering and perishing; the animal is like him in motion, perception and other attributes. As for ghayr, when annexed it is made indefinite, and when the annexation is cut off it may become definite; for when you say "ghayr Zayd" it becomes in extreme vagueness, since it encompasses countless things. But when you detach it from annexation, you may say "al-ghayr" and "al-mughayarah" are of one category, and likewise "al-taghayyur," so you make ghayr like the names of genera, or you make it a subject (mubtada') and intend by it a specific meaning.

The fourth: ﴿If they are truthful﴾ means in their saying ﴿He has invented it﴾ [al-Tur: 33]. We have mentioned that this refers back to what preceded: that he is a soothsayer, that he is a madman, that he is a poet, that he is an inventor. Had they been truthful in any of these, producing the like of the Qur'an would have been easy for them; and since they were unable, they lied in all of it.

The fifth discussion: We have mentioned that the Qur'an is miraculous, and there is no doubt about it, for the creatures were unable, when challenged, to produce anything close to it. Its being miraculous is either because of its eloquence, which is the view of the majority of the People of the Sunnah; or because God diverted the intellects of the intelligent from producing its like, and bound their tongues from uttering anything close to it, and prevented the capable from doing what is within their power—like one who performs an act no one else can do. For if someone says to another, "I will move this mountain," it is considered far-fetched from him; and likewise if he says, "I will do an act with which the creatures cannot lift an apple from its place," it is considered far-fetched from him. Each of these, when joined to the claim, is a miraculous act. This is the view of some theologians, and there is no flaw in it; and it may also be said that it is miraculous by both together.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ For this reason there is no disagreement that (أم) (am) does not mean (بل) (bal, "rather"). However, most exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir) hold that what is meant is the interrogative particle that occurs at the beginning of a sentence. It is either the hamza (همزة, the interrogative alif), so that it is as if he is saying: "Were they created from nothing?" or (هل) (hal, "is it that"). It may also be said that it is, in its original usage, the interrogative that occurs in the middle of a speech, and its implied form is: "Or were they created? Or were they created from nothing? Or are they the creators?" There are several issues here:

**The first issue:** How does this verse relate to what precedes it? We say: when they denied the Prophet ﷺ, attributed to him soothsaying, madness and poetry, and God cleared him of that, and He mentioned the proof of his truthfulness in refutation of their denial, He began with themselves, as if He were saying: "How can they deny him when within themselves is the proof of his truthfulness?" This is because his speech concerned three things: tawhid (divine oneness), resurrection (hashr), and prophethood (risalah). In themselves there is therefore that by which his truthfulness is known. The explanation is that they were created, and that is a proof of tawhid, because, as we have explained, in everything there is a sign indicating that He is One. We have explained its manner many times, so we will not repeat it.

As for resurrection, the first creation is a proof of the possibility and feasibility of the second creation. What we have mentioned is confirmed by God's concluding the interrogations with His saying: ﴿Or do they have a god other than God? Glory be to God above what they associate with Him﴾ [Al-Tur: 43].

**The second issue:** If the matter is as you have described, why was the phrase "Or were they created?" omitted? We say: because the negation of that is so evident that no room for dispute remains. If it is asked, "Why did He not begin with His saying 'Or were they created?' and then say 'Or were they created from nothing?'" we say: so that it may be known that before this there is a clearly negated matter, and what is mentioned here is close to it in the obviousness of its falsehood. If it is objected, "His saying ﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾ is also of obvious falsehood, since they know that they were created from dust, water and a drop (nutfah)," we say: the first is more evidently false, because the claim that they were not created is one whose proponent denies something necessary (darurah), so whoever denies it denies a matter that is self-evident.

**The third issue:** What is meant by His saying ﴿from nothing﴾? We say that there are several interpretations concerning it. The one transmitted is that they were created from nothing, without a creator. It was also said that they were created for no purpose, in vain. It was also said that they were created without a father or a mother. It may also be said: "Or were they created from nothing?" meaning: "Were they not created from dust or from water?" The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Did We not create you from a despised water?﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 20]. It may also be said that the second interrogation does not carry the meaning of negation but of affirmation. God, exalted, said: ﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creators?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 59], ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow, or are We the growers?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 64], ﴿Is it you who brought its tree into being, or are We the ones who bring it into being?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 72]. All of these, in the first part, are negated, and in the second part, affirmed. Likewise here God said: ﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾, meaning: the true one is this second alternative. This is like His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ [Al-Insan: 1].

If it is objected, "How can that be an affirmation, when the human being was created from dust?" we say: dust too was created from nothing. So when you look at the creation of the human being and trace his beginning, you find that he was created from nothing. Or we say that what is meant is: "Were they created from nothing that is mentioned or considered," namely the despised water.

**The fourth issue:** What is the purpose of mentioning the three matters in the verse? We say: they are ordered matters, each of which prevents acceptance of the doctrine of oneness and of resurrection, so He asked about them. He said: ﴿Or were they created at all?﴾, and for this reason they deny the doctrine of tawhid, because there is no origination (ijad), which is creation, and they deny resurrection because there is no first creation. ﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾ means: "Or do they say that they were created for no purpose, so there is no re-creation?" as He said: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 115].

According to our view that what is meant is "created neither from dust nor from water," this has a clear aspect, namely that when creation is not from something but is originative (ibda'i), its being created may be hidden from some dullards. For this reason some have said: "The heavens were raised by chance, and came into being without a creator." As for the human being, who is first a drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, then bone and flesh, no one can deny this after witnessing the changes of his states. So He said: ﴿Or were they created?﴾, in a manner in which the way of their creation would be hidden from them, by being created at the beginning without a prior state in which they were dust, water or a drop. It is not so; rather they were some of those things from which they were created in creation. So they were not created from nothing, such that they could deny oneness. For this reason He said: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾ [Al-Zumar: 6]. Accordingly God repeated His saying: ﴿We created man from a drop﴾ [Al-Insan: 2], and His saying: ﴿Did We not create you from a despised water?﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 20], which encompasses both matters mentioned in this place. For His saying ﴿Did We not create you from water?﴾ may mean the negation of the whole by negating creation, so that it is as if He said: "Were you created not from water?" According to the view of one who says that what is meant is: "Or were they created from nothing," that is, "from no creator," there is also a good order in it. This is because the negation of the Maker either means the negation of the world's being created, in which case it is not possible; or it is possible, but what is possible does not need an agent, so the possible would come into being without an influencing cause. Both of these are impossible.

As for His saying: ﴿Or are they the creators?﴾, its meaning is: "Are they the creators of creation?" Then the Creator would be wearied by the abundance of work, for man's habit is that he grows weary through creating. So if they say "Were they created?" then no god at all is established for them. Or "they were created, but the way of creation was hidden from them." Or "they made the Creator like themselves, and thereby attributed weakness to Him." Like His saying: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15]. This is in relation to resurrection. As for tawhid, it is a refutation of them, since they said: "Matters are diverse, and the diversity of effects indicates the diversity of causes." And they said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ [Sad: 5]. So God said: ﴿Or are they the creators?﴾, since the baker cannot sew and the tailor cannot build, and each is occupied by one affair to the exclusion of another.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Or were they created from nothing, or are they the creators [of themselves]? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather, they have no certainty.﴾ On this verse there are several interpretations:

The first: what al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) chose, namely that they do not have certainty that they were created. In this sense it is equivalent to His, exalted, saying: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Luqman: 25], meaning: they acknowledge that it is the creation of Allah, and not their own creation.

The second: the meaning is "Rather, they have no certainty that Allah is One." Its implied sense is: "The matter is not so," i.e., they were not created, but rather they lack certainty regarding the Oneness of Allah.

The third: they have no certainty at all, without mention of an object. It is said, "So-and-so is not a believer," and "So-and-so is not a disbeliever," to explain his position, even though no object is intended. Likewise the saying of the speaker, "So-and-so harms and pays [others]," to describe what is in him, not with the intention of mentioning an object. In this case its implied sense is: they did not create the heavens and the earth, and they do not have certainty regarding these proofs; rather they have no certainty at all, even if you bring them every sign. This is indicated by His, exalted, saying after that: ﴿And if they should see a piece of the sky falling, they would say, "Layered clouds."﴾ [al-Tur: 44]. This verse points to the proof from the horizons (al-afaq), while His saying earlier, ﴿Or were they created [from nothing]?﴾ [al-Tur: 35/37], is the proof from the selves (al-anfus).

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord, or are they the controllers?﴾ On this verse there are several interpretations:

The first: by "treasuries" is meant the treasuries of mercy.

The second: the treasuries of the unseen (al-ghayb).

The third: it refers to the hidden divine secrets that are concealed from beings.

The fourth: the treasuries of created things that man has never seen and has never heard of. The first and second of these interpretations are transmitted (manqul), while the third and fourth are derived by inference (mustanbat). His saying, ﴿or are they the controllers?﴾ completes the refutation of them. This is because when He said, ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ it indicates that they are not keepers of the mercy of Allah, so that they would know the treasuries of Allah. Yet the mere absence of their being keepers does not entail the absence of knowledge, since it is possible that one may oversee the storehouse; for knowledge of the treasuries belongs to the keeper and the scribe in the storehouse. So He said: you are neither keepers nor the scribes of the storehouse who hold authority over it. There is no difficulty in interpreting al-musaytirin (the controllers) as the scribes of the storehouse, since the root (s-t-r) indicates a line (satr), and this is used for writing. It has also been said that al-musaytir means "the one who has authority." It was read with the sad (ص) and likewise in many words that have the ta (ط), as in His saying: ﴿You are not a controller over them﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 22], where it has been read as musaytir.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen? Then let their listener bring a clear authority.﴾ This too is a completion of the proof, for one who is neither a keeper nor a scribe may still come to know a matter by hearing it from the keeper or the scribe. So He said: you are neither keepers nor scribes, nor have you met with them, because they are angels and there is no ascent for you to them. In this there are several issues:

First issue: The intended meaning is the negation of ascent. Yet negating a ladder for them does not necessarily entail negating ascent. What is the answer to this? We say: the negation is more emphatic than negating ascent, namely negating listening; and the end of the verse covers all of it, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Then let their listener bring a clear authority.﴾

Second issue: A ladder is not listened "in," rather one listens "on" it. What is the answer? We say, from two angles:

One: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that the meaning of ﴿they listen﴾ is "ascending upon it."

The second: what al-Wahidi mentioned, that "in" here means "on," as in His saying: ﴿And I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Taha: 71], i.e., on the trunks of palm trees. Both of these are weak, because of the implied supposition and alteration they involve.

Third issue: Why was the object of ﴿they listen﴾ omitted, and what is it? We say there are several views:

One: the thing listened to is the revelation, i.e., "Do they have a ladder by which they listen to the revelation?"

The second: they listen to what they say, that he is a poet, that Allah has a partner, and that the Gathering will not occur.

The third: the object is omitted altogether, as if he is saying: "Do they have the power of hearing from the heaven, so that they might know that he is not a messenger, and that his speech is not sent down?"

Fourth issue: He said ﴿then let their listener come﴾ and did not say "then let them come," as He, exalted, said: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾ [al-Tur: 34]. We say: He demanded of them what would be easier, on the supposition of their truthfulness, so that their gathering upon it would more clearly demonstrate the falsity of their claim. There He said ﴿then let them come﴾, i.e., gather together upon it, cooperate, and produce its like, for that is easier when they are together. As for ascending a ladder together, it is impossible, because only one can climb at a time, and only one attains the highest rung. Therefore He said ﴿then let [that one] come﴾, the one who was most advanced in ascent by what he heard.

Therefore He said: no, rather it is obligatory that he bring a proof that points to it.
