So He said: you are neither keepers nor scribes, nor have you met with them, because they are angels and there is no ascent for you to them. In this there are several issues:

First issue: The intended meaning is the negation of ascent. Yet negating a ladder for them does not necessarily entail negating ascent. What is the answer to this? We say: the negation is more emphatic than negating ascent, namely negating listening; and the end of the verse covers all of it, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Then let their listener bring a clear authority.﴾

Second issue: A ladder is not listened "in," rather one listens "on" it. What is the answer? We say, from two angles:

One: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that the meaning of ﴿they listen﴾ is "ascending upon it."

The second: what al-Wahidi mentioned, that "in" here means "on," as in His saying: ﴿And I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Taha: 71], i.e., on the trunks of palm trees. Both of these are weak, because of the implied supposition and alteration they involve.

Third issue: Why was the object of ﴿they listen﴾ omitted, and what is it? We say there are several views:

One: the thing listened to is the revelation, i.e., "Do they have a ladder by which they listen to the revelation?"

The second: they listen to what they say, that he is a poet, that Allah has a partner, and that the Gathering will not occur.

The third: the object is omitted altogether, as if he is saying: "Do they have the power of hearing from the heaven, so that they might know that he is not a messenger, and that his speech is not sent down?"

Fourth issue: He said ﴿then let their listener come﴾ and did not say "then let them come," as He, exalted, said: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾ [al-Tur: 34]. We say: He demanded of them what would be easier, on the supposition of their truthfulness, so that their gathering upon it would more clearly demonstrate the falsity of their claim. There He said ﴿then let them come﴾, i.e., gather together upon it, cooperate, and produce its like, for that is easier when they are together. As for ascending a ladder together, it is impossible, because only one can climb at a time, and only one attains the highest rung. Therefore He said ﴿then let [that one] come﴾, the one who was most advanced in ascent by what he heard.

Fifth issue: His saying ﴿with a clear authority﴾: what is meant by it? We say it is an indication of a subtle point, namely that if they were asked to bring what they had heard, and it were said to them ﴿then let their listener come with what he heard﴾, then any one of them could say, "I heard such and such," and thus fabricate a lie. Therefore He said: no, rather it is obligatory that he bring a proof that points to it.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Has He taken daughters for Himself, while you have sons?﴾ This is an indication of the negation of partnership (shirk) and the corruption of what they say, by another way. It is that the one who disposes of affairs only needs a partner because of his incapacity, whereas God is All-Powerful, so He has no partner. They said: "We do not make these idols and others partners; rather we venerate them because they are the daughters of God." So God Most High said: How can you attribute daughters to God, when the creation of daughters and sons is only for the possibility of the person's passing away? Were it not for procreation, offspring would be cut off and the origin would be lifted up, without the succession (fasl) taking its place. So God decreed procreation, and for this reason there is no childbirth in Paradise, because the abode is the abode of permanence, in which there is no death for the fathers, so that the building is not maintained by the coming into being of children. When this is established, a child exists only in a state where the father's passing away is possible. For this reason God Most High said at the beginning of the Surah of Al 'Imran: ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2], meaning: He is Living and does not die, so He does not need a child to inherit from Him, and He is Self-Subsisting, not changing and not weakening, so He does not need a child to take His place. This was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran. Then God Most High clarified this in the most eloquent manner, and said that they attribute daughters to Him, and attribute sons to themselves, although attributing daughters to them would be more appropriate. That is because a large number of daughters helps to a large number of offspring, since many females can be impregnated by one male with many children. As for many males, one female cannot be impregnated by them with children. Do you not see that among sheep, females are rarely slaughtered? This is because it has been established that preserving the species through the female is more beneficial with regard to multiplication. So God Most High said: "I am the Self-Subsisting, who has no end, and I have no need for the preservation of the species through the coming into being of individuals, whereas you are exposed to swift death, and the preservation of the world is through females more so; and you disown them, while God Most High is free of that, and you attribute daughters to Him." Based on this, what preceded was an indication of the negation of a partner in view of His having no beginning, and this is an indication of the negation of a partner in view of His having no end. If it is asked: how did the attribution of daughters to God Most High occur to them, although this is a matter of utmost ugliness that is not hidden from any rational person, and these people possessed intellects, which are the basis of obligation, and that degree is sufficient for knowing the corruption of this saying? We say: that saying was prompted in them by following reason and disregarding transmitted revelation. Their position in this matter is the position of the philosophers, who say: the clear intellect must be followed, and they say transmitted revelation is irrelevant and is not followed unless it agrees with reason; and if it agrees, then transmitted revelation has no weight, because reason there is sufficient. Then they said: the begetter is called a father because he is the cause of the existence of the child; hence it is said when something appears from something: "this was generated from that." So they say fever is generated from the corruption of humours. They said: God Most High is the cause of the existence of the angels, a necessary cause without choice, so they named Him "father," and did not consider the obligation to exalt God above naming Him with what gives the impression of deficiency, nor the obligation to restrict His names to the most beautiful names that the Law has revealed, because they did not give weight to transmitted revelation. So they said it is permissible to apply metaphorical and literal names to God Most High and His attributes; so they named Him "lover" and "beloved," and named Him "father" and "begetter," but they did not name Him "son" or "begotten," by their unanimous agreement; and that is misguidance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 52, verse 40:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so that they are burdened with debt?﴾

The connection is that when the polytheists discarded the Law (shar') and followed what they supposed to be reason ('aql), and they named the thing that comes into existence after non-existence a "born" and a "begotten," and the Originator a "father," then disbelief and associating partners with God necessarily followed from this. So He said to them: What is it that compels you to discard the Law and abandon following the Messenger (ﷺ)? Is it because he asks you for something? Then they could not say anything but "yes," and there remained for them only to say "no." So we say to them: How have you followed the saying of the philosopher, which permits you falsehood and which necessitates treating the side of God, Exalted is He, lightly in wording, if it has no meaning, as you claim? And you do not follow the one who commands you to justice in meaning and to goodness in wording, and who says to you: follow the clear, true meaning, and use the good, well-mannered wording? This is in the utmost beauty of exegesis, and in it there are several issues:

The first issue: What is the benefit in the questioning of the Prophet (ﷺ) where He said "Or do you ask them" and did not say "Or are they asked for a payment," as He said: ﴿Or do they say﴾ [Yunus: 38] and He said: ﴿Or do they intend a plot﴾ [al-Tur: 42], and so on? We say that in it there are two benefits:

The first: consoling the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ). For when they refused to listen and disdained to follow, it was difficult for the Prophet (ﷺ), so his Lord said to him: You have brought what is incumbent upon you, so let not your chest be constricted because they did not believe. You are not blameworthy. You would only be blamed had you asked them for a payment. Did you ask them for that, so that it burdened them? No. Then there is no blame upon you.

The second: that had He said "Or are they asked," it would have implied a payment in general, and that is not the case. For they used to associate partners and demand payment from their leaders. As for the Prophet (ﷺ), He said to him: You do not ask them for a payment, for they do not follow you; others ask them, and they are asked and follow those who ask. And this is the utmost of misguidance.

The second issue: If someone says: you have obliged yourself to show that "am" (or) never occurs except as connecting, actually or implicitly, so how is that here? We say: it is as if He, Exalted, said: Do you guide them for the sake of God's countenance, or do you ask them for a payment? He omitted the first because the denial does not fall upon it, as we said regarding His words ﴿Or has He daughters?﴾, that the measure is one, "or has He daughters?" He omitted mention of the first because the denial from God, Exalted is He, does not fall upon it, and because they were saying that he does not intend the countenance of God, Exalted is He, but intends only leadership and payment in this world.

The third issue: Is there in the specific wording of His words, Exalted is He, "a payment" (ajran), a benefit not found in other wording, had He said "Do you ask them something, or wealth, or other than that?" We say: yes. It has been stated earlier that every word in the Qur'an has a benefit, even if we do not know it. What appears here is that it is an indication that what the Prophet (ﷺ) brings contains their welfare. For a payment is only sought when one does something from which the one sought benefits. So He said: You have brought them what, if you had asked a payment for it, and they knew the full extent of the benefit in your call for them and through them, they would have come to you with all their wealth and ransomed you with their own selves. And yet you do not ask them for a payment. Had He said "something" or "wealth," this benefit would not have been achieved. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: This indicates that he did not ask them for any payment at all. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any payment, except the affection among kinsfolk﴾ [al-Shura: 23] seem to indicate that he asked for some payment. How then is the combination of the two? We say: there is no discrepancy between them; rather, both are true and both are like one speech. Its explanation is that what is meant by His words ﴿except the affection among kinsfolk﴾ [al-Shura: 23] is: I do not ask you for any payment that returns to this world; rather, my payment is love in nearness to God, Exalted is He, and that the perfect servants of God are nearer to God, Exalted is He, than His deficient servants, and the servants of God whom God spoke to, and who spoke to Him, and whom He sent to perfect His servants, and who became perfected, are nearer to God than those whom [He did not speak to] and whom God did not send and who did not become perfected. On this basis it has the meaning of His words ﴿My reward is only from God﴾ [Hud: 29], and to Him I belong. And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed I shall boast of you among the nations on the Day of Resurrection." And His words ﴿so that they are burdened with debt﴾. Between what we have mentioned: His words ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment﴾ mean the reward of this world, and His words ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any payment﴾ mean generality, then He made an exception. There is no need for what al-Wahidi said, that it is a disjunctive exception, meaning "but [I ask for] the affection among kinsfolk." We have mentioned it there, so let it be sought from there.

The fifth issue: His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so that they are burdened with debt﴾ indicate that he (ﷺ) asked them for nothing. Even had he asked them for some payment, it would not have been permissible for them to abandon following him for the least thing, except if the obligation burdened them and took all that they have, and prevented them from remaining behind, so that debt weighs upon them after nothing of their substance remains.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write it down?﴾ This is in the order we have mentioned. It is as if God, exalted is He, were saying to them: "On what basis have you discarded the Sharia and its excellences, and said what you have said, relying on your following of corrupt illusions which you call rational notions? The Prophet ﷺ does not ask you for a wage, and you do not know. So you have no excuse, for an excuse is either a matter of burden (ghuramah, financial obligation) or a matter of having no need for what he has brought. There is no burden upon you in it, and you have no independence from it." There are several issues here:

The first issue: How is the estimation (taqdir) to be understood? We say there is no need for an estimation; rather, it is an interrogative in the middle position, as we have mentioned. It is as if He said: "Do you guide them for the sake of God, exalted is He, or do you ask them for a wage so that they refuse, or do they have no need for what you say, because they have the unseen and therefore do not follow?"

The second issue: Is the alif and lam in "al-ghayb" (the unseen) for defining the genus (li-l-jins) or for a specific reference (li-'ahd)? We say the apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the kind of the unseen, just as the speaker says "he bought the meat," meaning to clarify the reality of eating meat, not a specific piece of meat. The intended sense in His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the seen﴾ [al-An'am: 73] is the genus, and it encompasses every unseen matter.

The third issue: On this basis, how is it valid to say "the unseen is with them," when what is with a person cannot be unseen? We say its meaning is that what was hidden from others was present before them. It has also been said that this is connected to His saying ﴿We await for him the vicissitudes of time﴾, i.e., "Do you have the unseen, so that you know that he will die before you?" But this is weak, because that is a distant matter to be mentioned here, or because His saying ﴿Say: Wait﴾ is connected to it, and that prevents this from being connected to that.

The fourth issue: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿so that they write it down﴾? We say it is the clarification of the matter, and an indication that what the Prophet ﷺ has of knowledge of the unseen, he knew through revelation, matters, secrets, rulings and reports in great number, all of which he is certain of, and it is not like the speculation of the physiognomist (al-mutafarrisi) who says "the matter is such and such." If it is said to him, "Write with your hand that it will happen," he refuses and says, "I do not claim certainty or definiteness in it, but I mention it as such and such by way of conjecture and inference." Whereas if he were certain, he would say, "Write this from me, and record in the registers that on such and such a day such and such will occur." So His saying ﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write it down?﴾ means: "Have they reached the rank of Muhammad ﷺ, so that they have become independent of him and turned away?" It is related from Ibn Qutaybah that the intended sense of "writing" is judgment, meaning "they judge." He relied on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Judge between us by the Book of God," meaning the ruling of God. But that is not the intended meaning; rather, it is from the class of ellipsis (al-idmar), meaning "by what is in the Book of God, exalted is He." It is said: "So-and-so judges according to the school of al-Shafi'i," meaning according to what is in it. And the messenger who carries the king's letter says to the subjects: "Act by the king's letter."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they intend a scheme? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared by the scheme.﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: What is the connection and relevance between the two statements? We say it is clarified by explaining the intended meaning of His words ﴿Or do they intend a scheme?﴾ Some exegetes said: "Or do they intend to scheme against you? Then they are the ones who will be ensnared," meaning they are not able to scheme, for God protects you with His watchfulness and grants you victory by His safeguarding. In accordance with this, if we say, following the view of one who says that ﴿Or do they have the unseen?﴾ is connected to His words, ﴿We await for him the vicissitudes of time﴾, then there is an arrangement of supreme excellence in it, namely that when they said, ﴿We await for him the vicissitudes of time,﴾ it was said to them: "Do you know the unseen, so that you know that he will die before you? Or do you intend a scheme, so that you say, 'We will kill him,' and he dies before us?" If you claim knowledge of the unseen, then you are liars; and if you think that you are able to do it, then you are mistaken, for God protects him from you and grants him victory over you. As for what we said, that what is meant is that he, peace and blessings be upon him, does not ask you for wealth in return for guidance while you do not know what he brought, were it not for his guidance, since it is among the unseen matters, then we say there are several aspects to it:

The first: The intended meaning of His words, ﴿Or do they intend a scheme?﴾ is, that is, from Satan and his misleading, so that their desire is fulfilled. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "You do not ask them for a reward, and they know the unseen, so they are in need of you, yet they turned away. They have chosen the scheme of Satan and been pleased with his misleading." Here "intending" means "choosing" and "loving," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth﴾ [al-Shura: 20], and as He said: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?﴾ [al-Saffat: 86]. Even clearer than that is His words: ﴿Indeed, I desire that you bear my sin and your sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 29].

The second aspect: It may be said that the intended meaning, and God knows best, is: "Or do they intend a scheme against God? It will reach them, and they will soon be ensnared." The arrangement of the speech is that, since there is no longer any proof left for their turning away, they desire the descent of punishment upon them, while God has sent to them a messenger who asks them for no reward and guides them to what they have no knowledge of and no book with them, yet they turn away. So they then intend to destroy him and scheme against him, because enticement (istidraj) is a scheme, and granting respite is for increasing sin. Thus it is said that this is not corrupt, because the words "scheme" and "harm" are not applied to the act of God except by way of reciprocity, and likewise "plotting." So one does not say "God harmed the disbelievers" or "God transgressed," unless something of that kind was first mentioned concerning them, and then, because of it, a similar word is used with regard to God, as in His words: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and He said: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194], and He said: ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], and He said: ﴿They are plotting a plot, and I am plotting a plot﴾ [al-Tariq: 15, 16]. For we say: a scheme is that which harms the one upon whom it descends, even if it is good when it proceeds from the one who does it. Do you not see that Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And by God, I will surely scheme against your idols after you have turned and gone away﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57], without any reciprocity.

The second issue: What is the benefit in His words, ﴿But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared by the scheme,﴾ and what is the difference between the meaning of this statement and the meaning of someone's saying: "Or do they intend a scheme, then they are the ones who will be ensnared"? We say: the benefit is that the disbeliever is ensnared in return for his disbelief, not in return for his intending the scheme. Had He said, "Or do they intend a scheme, then they are the ones who will be ensnared," it would have been understood from it that if they did not intend it, they would not be ensnared. This supports what we have mentioned, that what is meant by the scheme is the scheme of Satan or the scheme of God, meaning His punishment of them, because His words ﴿But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared﴾ are general for every disbeliever whom Satan has deceived and whom God schemes against, that is, punishes. The meaning, according to what we have mentioned, becomes: "Do you guide them for the sake of God, or do you ask them for a reward so that it burdens them and they refuse to follow? Or do they have the unseen, so they have no need of you and turn away from you? Or is it that neither of these two last matters applies, so they desire punishment? Punishment is not averted from them in any way because of their disbelief. Thus those who disbelieve are punished."

The third issue: What is the benefit of the indefiniteness of "scheme," since He did not say "Or do they intend your scheme," or "the scheme," or something else, so as to remove the ambiguity? We say there is a benefit in it, which is an indication of the punishment befalling them from where they do not perceive. It is as if He said: "It will come upon them suddenly, and they will have no knowledge of it." Or it is for the sake of magnifying it, as we have mentioned many times.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Or do they have a god other than Allah? Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ He repeated the affirmation of divine unity, and it conveys the same point as His words: ﴿Or has He daughters while you have sons?﴾ [al-Tur: 39]. Regarding "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah) there is a noble discussion: the lexicographers said that *subhan* is a proper noun (*ism 'alam*) for glorification (*al-tasbih*). We have already mentioned this in our commentary on His words: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17], and we elaborated on its benefits. If it is said: it is permissible to say that *Subhan Allah* is a verbal noun (*ism masdar*), and to say *subhan* on the pattern *fu'lan*, so that *subhan* is mentioned without being placed in the position of the glorification of Allah, as is said in glorification (*al-tasbih*), we answer: that is like the statement of the speaker: *min* is a prepositional particle (*harf jarr*) and *fi* is an adverb of place (*kalimat zarf*), where it is predicated about them, although a particle is not predicated about. The answer is that *min* and *fi* in this context were made like nouns and were not left in their original usage, as in your saying: "I took from Zayd," and "the dirham is in the purse." Likewise, *subhan* in the cases mentioned was not left in the places where it is used, for in that context it was not left as a proper noun, just as it is said that Zayd is on the pattern *fa'l*. This differs from *al-tasbih* in what we have mentioned.

The fourth issue: the *ma* in His words ﴿of what they associate﴾ may have two interpretations:

First: that it is a verbal (*masdariyyah*) particle, meaning: He is glorified above their associating.

Second: that it is a relative (*khabariyyah*) particle, meaning: above those whom they associate. On this reading it may refer to offspring, because they used to say that the daughters belong to Allah, so He said: Glory be to Allah above the daughters and sons. It may also refer to the likeness of the deities, because they used to say that He is like what they worship, so He said: Glory be to Allah above what they worship as a likeness.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And if they see a fragment of the sky falling, they will say: "A layered cloud."﴾

The order here is that when He, exalted, made clear the corruption of their statements and their falling from the level of consideration, He indicated that they had no remaining ground for excuse. The signs had appeared and the proofs had been distinguished, yet they did not believe. After that, ﴿if they see a fragment of the sky falling, they will say: a cloud,﴾ meaning they will deny the sign. But when a sign is manifested in the most manifest of things, it becomes more manifest. Its explanation is this: whoever brings an object from inside his house and claims that he did such-and-such with it, the listener may suppose that it is in his house and that he did not create it. But when he says to the people, "Bring me an object of your choosing, so that I may do for you such-and-such with it," that suspicion disappears. The most manifest thing to a human being, however, is the earth, which is his cradle and bedding, and the sky, which is his roof and canopy. The Arabs were, in their fundamental doctrine, upon the view of the philosophers, and one does not turn to the words of the philosopher who says: "We declare Him utterly transcendent, so that we do not permit His being seen or His being described by an attribute beyond His essence, so that He is one in reality." How then would our doctrine be the doctrine of one who associates with Allah a carved idol? We say: when you attributed events to the stars and began calling upon the stars, the ignorant took this from you and adopted it as a doctrine. And since it is established that the Arabs in the pre-Islamic period were originally upon the doctrine of the philosophers, who speak of the natures (*al-taba'i'*), they say: the earth's nature is generation, and the sky's nature prevents separation and detachment. So Allah, exalted, responded to them in several places: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or We shall cause a fragment of the sky to fall upon them﴾ [Saba': 9], nullifying the natures and affirming choice in events. Here He said: if We bring something extremely strange, in the most manifest of things, which is the sky that they always see, and they know that no one reaches it to count, by medicines or otherwise, what must cause its fall, they would deny it. How much more so in matters less than that.

What supports what we have mentioned, and that they were upon the philosophers' doctrine concerning the sky, is that they said: ﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ [al-Isra': 92], meaning: that is possible in your claim, but for us it is not. *Al-kisfah* is a piece; one says "a *kisfah* of cloth," meaning a piece. There are discussions concerning it:

First discussion: He used the word *kisf* for the sky. The lexicographers mentioned its usage for cloth, because Allah, exalted, likened the sky to a spread-out garment. For this reason He mentioned it earlier, saying: ﴿And the heavens are folded up﴾ [al-Zumar: 67], and He said: ﴿On the day We roll up the sky﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104].

Second discussion: He used *kisf* for the sky and *khasf* for the earth, saying: ﴿We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾ [Saba': 9]. This indicates the view of those who say that one says *khusuf* of the moon and *kusuf* of the sun. The reason is that the point of articulation of the *kha'* is lower than that of the *kaf*, and the point of the *kaf* is above it, adjacent to it. So they used the descriptor of the lower for the lower and the higher for the higher. Thus they said *kusuf* and *kasf* for the sun and the sky, and *khusuf* and *khasf* for the moon and the earth. This is of the same kind as their saying regarding *al-matih* and *al-mayih* (the one drawing water and the one drawing it up): that the dot placed above is for the one above the well, and the dot placed below is according to those who permit placing it below for the one at the bottom of the well.

Third discussion: He said of the clouds: ﴿and We make it fragments﴾, although it is beneath the moon, and He said of the moon: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 8]. That is because during an eclipse the moon has a counterpart above it, which is the sun during a solar eclipse. The cloud was considered in relation to the people of the earth, who look at it. So for the moon He did not say *khasf* in relation to the cloud, but it was said in relation to the sun, and for the cloud it was said in relation to the earth.

Second issue: *saqitan* (falling) may have two interpretations:

First: that it is a second object (*maf'ul thani*), as one says: "I saw Zayd knowledgeable."

Second: that it is a circumstantial state (*hal*), as one says: "I struck him standing." The second is more appropriate, because seeing, when it takes two objects, mostly means knowing. One says: "I see this doctrine as correct" and "I see this aspect as clear." When it takes one object, it mostly means seeing with the eye. One says: "I saw Zayd." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿When they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 84], and He said: ﴿If you see any human being﴾ [Maryam: 26]. The intended meaning in the verse is seeing with the eye.

Third issue: in His words ﴿falling﴾ there is a benefit that is not obtained without falling. That is because in their view the heavens cannot be separated, and it is not possible for them to descend or come down. So He said *saqitan* (falling), to oppose what they believe in two respects: the first is separation, and the second is falling. Had He said "a separated fragment" or "a suspended fragment," this benefit would not have been obtained.

Fourth issue: in His words ﴿they will say﴾ there is another benefit, because it shows the obstinacy that is the aim of the recitation of this verse. At that time they devise pretexts so that they are not bound to submit, so they say "a cloud," a statement without conviction. His words ﴿layered (*markum*)﴾ mean that part of it is piled upon part, as if they are repelling what is raised against them, that a cloud is like air and does not prevent a body from passing through it. This is the strongest objection, so they say that it is a heap (*rukam*), and thus it became solid and strong.

Sixth issue: the omission of the demonstrative word, where He did not say "they will say: this." This indicates the clarity of the matter and the manifestness of the obstinacy, so they do not find it becoming to say what leaves no room for dispute. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Or do they have a god other than Allah? On this reading it may refer to offspring, because they used to say that the daughters belong to Allah, so He said: Glory be to Allah above the daughters and sons. It may also refer to the likeness of the deities, because they used to say that He is like what they worship, so He said: Glory be to Allah above what they worship as a likeness.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And if they see a fragment of the sky falling, they will say: "A layered cloud."﴾

The order here is that when He, exalted, made clear the corruption of their statements and their falling from the level of consideration, He indicated that they had no remaining ground for excuse. The signs had appeared and the proofs had been distinguished, yet they did not believe. After that, ﴿if they see a fragment of the sky falling, they will say: a cloud,﴾ meaning they will deny the sign. But when a sign is manifested in the most manifest of things, it becomes more manifest. Its explanation is this: whoever brings an object from inside his house and claims that he did such-and-such with it, the listener may suppose that it is in his house and that he did not create it. But when he says to the people, "Bring me an object of your choosing, so that I may do for you such-and-such with it," that suspicion disappears. The most manifest thing to a human being, however, is the earth, which is his cradle and bedding, and the sky, which is his roof and canopy. The Arabs were, in their fundamental doctrine, upon the view of the philosophers, and one does not turn to the words of the philosopher who says: "We declare Him utterly transcendent, so that we do not permit His being seen or His being described by an attribute beyond His essence, so that He is one in reality." How then would our doctrine be the doctrine of one who associates with Allah a carved idol? We say: when you attributed events to the stars and began calling upon the stars, the ignorant took this from you and adopted it as a doctrine. And since it is established that the Arabs in the pre-Islamic period were originally upon the doctrine of the philosophers, who speak of the natures (*al-taba'i'*), they say: the earth's nature is generation, and the sky's nature prevents separation and detachment. So Allah, exalted, responded to them in several places: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or We shall cause a fragment of the sky to fall upon them﴾ [Saba': 9], nullifying the natures and affirming choice in events. Here He said: if We bring something extremely strange, in the most manifest of things, which is the sky that they always see, and they know that no one reaches it to count, by medicines or otherwise, what must cause its fall, they would deny it. How much more so in matters less than that.

What supports what we have mentioned, and that they were upon the philosophers' doctrine concerning the sky, is that they said: ﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ [al-Isra': 92], meaning: that is possible in your claim, but for us it is not. *Al-kisfah* is a piece; one says "a *kisfah* of cloth," meaning a piece. There are discussions concerning it:

First discussion: He used the word *kisf* for the sky. The lexicographers mentioned its usage for cloth, because Allah, exalted, likened the sky to a spread-out garment. For this reason He mentioned it earlier, saying: ﴿And the heavens are folded up﴾ [al-Zumar: 67], and He said: ﴿On the day We roll up the sky﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104].

Second discussion: He used *kisf* for the sky and *khasf* for the earth, saying: ﴿We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾ [Saba': 9]. This indicates the view of those who say that one says *khusuf* of the moon and *kusuf* of the sun. The reason is that the point of articulation of the *kha'* is lower than that of the *kaf*, and the point of the *kaf* is above it, adjacent to it. So they used the descriptor of the lower for the lower and the higher for the higher. Thus they said *kusuf* and *kasf* for the sun and the sky, and *khusuf* and *khasf* for the moon and the earth. This is of the same kind as their saying regarding *al-matih* and *al-mayih* (the one drawing water and the one drawing it up): that the dot placed above is for the one above the well, and the dot placed below is according to those who permit placing it below for the one at the bottom of the well.

Third discussion: He said of the clouds: ﴿and We make it fragments﴾, although it is beneath the moon, and He said of the moon: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 8]. That is because during an eclipse the moon has a counterpart above it, which is the sun during a solar eclipse. The cloud was considered in relation to the people of the earth, who look at it. So for the moon He did not say *khasf* in relation to the cloud, but it was said in relation to the sun, and for the cloud it was said in relation to the earth.

Second issue: *saqitan* (falling) may have two interpretations:

First: that it is a second object (*maf'ul thani*), as one says: "I saw Zayd knowledgeable."

One says: "I see this doctrine as correct" and "I see this aspect as clear." When it takes one object, it mostly means seeing with the eye. One says: "I saw Zayd." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 52, verse 45:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So leave them until they encounter their Day, in which they will be struck senseless﴾. That is: when it has become clear that they will not return, then leave them until they encounter it. There are several issues (masa'il) in this.

The First Issue: (فَذَرْهُمْ) (fadharhum, "so leave them") is an imperative. It would seem that this means the Prophet ﷺ no longer had permission to invite them to Islam, but this is not so. The answer to this is in several respects.

The first: these verses, like His saying ﴿So turn away﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:30] and ﴿Turn away from them﴾ [al-Saffat 37:78], and others besides them, are all abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of fighting (ayat al-qital). This is weak.

The second: the intended meaning is not a command but a threat, as a master says to someone who advises him about his guilty slave: "Leave him, for he will receive the consequence of his crime."

The third: the intended meaning is those who are obstinate, who are not specified, and the Prophet ﷺ used to call people in general. It is possible that the address is intended for those whose obstinacy has not become apparent, not for those whose obstinacy has become apparent; so God did not say (fadharhum) concerning them. This is supported by the fact that He, exalted is He, said earlier: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur 52:29], and then said here (fadharhum). The one who is reminded is therefore the fearful ones, who said ﴿Indeed, we were before among our people fearful﴾ [al-Tur 52:26], and the one who is left is those who said ﴿A poet, for whom we await the misfortunes of time﴾ [al-Tur 52:30], and so on besides that.

The Second Issue: (حَتَّى) (hatta, "until") indicates the endpoint (lil-ghayah). It is as if He, exalted is He, had said: leave them until that day, and do not speak to them, then on that day renew the speech and say: "Did I not tell you that the Hour is coming, that reckoning is established and punishment endures? So do not speak to them until that day, then speak to them in order to inform them."

The second: the intended meaning of (hatta) is the endpoint in which the particle (lam) is used, as one says: "Do not feed him until he dies," meaning "so that he dies" (li-yamuta). This is because the (lam) of purpose is where the action of the purpose ends, so the meaning of endpoint and the meaning of causation both exist in it. It is permissible to use both words in this way. Perhaps the intended meaning of His saying ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr 15:99] is this, that is, until certainty comes to you. If it is said: "Whoever does not leave them will also encounter that day," we say: the intended meaning of His saying ﴿they will be struck senseless﴾ is that they will be destroyed, so the warner, the fearful one, is not destroyed, and he is excluded from them, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be struck senseless, except whom God wills﴾ [al-Zumar 39:68]. We have already mentioned there that whoever acknowledges the truth and knows that the Day of Reckoning is coming, when the Blast occurs, is like one who knows that the thunder will roll and prepares to hear it, while one who does not know is like the heedless. When the Blast occurs, the heedless one trembles, but the one who knows does not tremble. At that point, the threat is of encountering their day, because every person encounters his day; it is only the encounter with their day in which they are struck senseless, that is, the day described with this attribute. This is like His saying: ﴿Had it not been that a blessing from his Lord had reached him, he would have been cast out onto the open plain while he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Qalam 68:49]. The negated thing is not being cast onto the open plain, because that has already occurred, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿So We cast him onto the open plain while he was sick﴾ [al-Saffat 37:145]. What is negated is the casting out in which he is blameworthy, and this did not occur.

The Third Issue: (حَتَّى) sometimes makes what follows it in the future tense in the subjunctive (yunsabu) and sometimes in the indicative (yurfa'u). The distinction between them is that when the verb is future and awaited and does not occur at present, it is in the subjunctive. You say: "I studied jurisprudence until my rank rises," for you are awaiting it. If it is present, it is in the indicative. You say: "I repeat until my strength fails, then I sleep." The reason for this is that (hatta) of the future indicates the endpoint, and (lam) of causation indicates purpose, and purpose is the endpoint of the action. You say: "Why are you building the house?" He says: "For dwelling." So his saying (hatta turfa'a, "until it is raised") becomes like his saying (li-arfa'a, "so that I may raise"), and both contain an implied (an, "that"). If it is said: "You have said nothing, and you have not mentioned the cause of the subjunctive when the future is intended and the indicative when the present is intended," we say: when the future verb is awaited and is before the eye and held in the mind, watching for it, it is treated in its wording as what is in its meaning. For this reason they said concerning the construct (idafah) that the governing noun, when it draws one thing toward another in meaning, is shortened in form. What supports what we have mentioned is that the verb is put in the subjunctive only after (an, "that"), (lan, "never"), (kay, "in order that") and (idhan, "then"), and the pure futurity of the verb in these positions is necessary. The particle that makes the verb refer to the present prevents the subjunctive, so you cannot say: "Indeed, so-and-so is hitting," with a subjunctive. If it is said: "The (sin) and (sawfa) make the verb purely future, yet they do not put it in the subjunctive, and they prevent subjunctive by an operator," as in His saying: ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:20], we say: (sawfa) and (sin) are not different in meaning except in restricting the verb to the future, while (an) and (lan) have a meaning that is valid only in the future. Thus by (sin) only futurity is established, and no meaning in the future is established by it. What is awaited is what is in the future, not futurity itself. An example of this: when you say, "I worship God so that He may forgive me," (kay) establishes a purpose, which is forgiveness, and it is in the future of time. When you say, "I ask forgiveness of You, my Lord," (sin) establishes the futurity of forgiveness. There is a difference between what the speech intends to demonstrate as futurity, but futurity exists only within a meaning, so one brings in the meaning in order to show the futurity through it, and between what the speech intends as a meaning in the future. Thus you mention the futurity in order to show the locus of your intended point.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 52, verse 46:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day when their cunning will avail them nothing, nor will they be helped.﴾

Page 234

When He said ﴿they will meet their Day﴾ [al-Tur: 45], and every righteous and wicked person meets his day, He repeated the description of their day and mentioned what distinguishes their day from the day of the believers, saying: ﴿on the Day when it will not avail them﴾. It differs from the day of the believers, for the Exalted said of it: ﴿This is a Day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. There are several issues in this:

The first issue: regarding ﴿on the Day when it will not avail﴾ there are two aspects:

The first: it is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿their Day﴾.

The second: it is an adverbial complement (zarf) of ﴿they will meet﴾, meaning: they will meet their Day on a Day. If it is said: this entails that the day is within a day, so the day would be an adverbial complement of the day, we say: it is in the manner of the statement of one who says: "The day of the killing of so-and-so will come on the day when his crimes are made clear." There is no impediment to this. We have already discussed the question of time and its permissibility as an adverbial complement in the Exalted's saying ﴿on that Day﴾ (yawma'idhin), and the permissibility of attributing a day to time even though it is a time.

The second issue: the Exalted said ﴿on the Day when their cunning will not avail them﴾, and He did not say "on the Day when their cunning will not avail them" (yughnihim), although "al-ighna'" transitively takes its object directly, for a great benefit: the speaker's saying "aghnani kadha" is understood to mean that it benefited me, whereas his saying "aghna 'anni" is understood to mean that it warded off harm from me. This is because his saying "aghnani" in reality means "it provided me with benefit without my needing it," whereas his saying "aghna 'anni" means "it did not make me need to be present, so another made my presence unnecessary." One who is summoned for a matter says: "Take my son in my stead (khudhu 'anni waladi), for he will suffice in my place (yughni 'anni)," meaning he will suffice you in my place, thereby also warding off from me the hardship of presence. So His saying ﴿it will not avail them﴾ means it does not ward off harm from them. There is no doubt that His saying "it does not ward off harm from them" is more eloquent than "it does not benefit them." Had He said "on the Day when their truthfulness will avail them" regarding the believers, it would not have conveyed their benefit, so He said ﴿a Day when the truthful will benefit﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119], as if He had said "on the Day when their truthfulness will avail them." Thus He used "yughnihim" for the believers and "la yughni 'anhum" for the disbelievers. This is something only one who possesses a share of the science of eloquence (ilm al-bayan), and who reflects upon the verses of God with a blazing intellect, will perceive, and may God grant him success.

The third issue: the original order is to place the agent before the object, and to place the pronoun before the noun. As for the first, it is because the agent is attached to the verb; for this reason they said "fa'altu" and they made the lam quiescent, so that four moving vowels would not occur in one word. They said "darabaka" without making it quiescent, because the kaf is the pronoun of the object and is detached. As for placing the pronoun first, it is because it is more concise: when you say "darabani Zayd" it is closer to brevity than your saying "daraba Zayd iyyaya." If there is no brevity, as in your saying "marra bi Zayd" and "marra bi," then placing the agent first is preferable. Here, had He said "on the Day when their cunning will not avail them" (yughnihim kaydu-hum), placing the object first would have been better; but when He said "on the Day when their cunning will not avail them" (la yughni 'anhum kaydu-hum), it became like what we said of "marra Zayd bi." Why, then, did He not place the agent first? We say: there is a benefit derived from the science of eloquence, namely that placing the more important first is preferable. Had He said "on the Day when their cunning will not avail," a hearer of this speech might say: "their cunning does not avail others," and so hope for good for them; but when he hears "will not avail them," his hope is cut off and he awaits the matter that will not avail.

The fourth issue: we have mentioned that the meaning of kayd (cunning) is an action that harms the one upon whom it falls, even if it is good when issued from its doer. What is the benefit in specifying the act that harms by mention, and why did He not say "on the Day when their deeds will not avail them" in general? We say: this is an analogy by way of priority (qiyas bi'l-tariq al-awla), because they used to perform the deeds of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, and they believed that these were the best of their deeds. So He said: what avails them nothing is their best deeds, in which they believed, so as to cut off their hope in what is lesser than that. There is another aspect: when He said earlier ﴿or do they intend a plot?﴾ and we have stated that most exegetes hold that it refers to their scheming to kill the Prophet ﷺ, He said ﴿they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾, meaning their cunning does not benefit them in this world, so what will they do on a Day when that cunning will not benefit them but rather harm them? And His saying ﴿nor will they be helped﴾

In it there are several aspects:

The first: it completes the explanation. Its aspect is that the one who summons first arranges matters to ward off the disliked outcome so that he does not need to seek help from others or to be obligated to them; then, if that does not benefit him, he seeks help from outsiders. So He said: the deeds of their own selves do not benefit them, nor does anyone help them when despair sets in and their despair of their own turning toward Him is complete.

The second: its meaning is the same as the meaning of the Exalted's saying ﴿Their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they save me﴾ [Ya-Sin: 23]. So His saying ﴿on the Day when their cunning will avail them nothing﴾ means their worship of idols; and their saying ﴿These are our intercessors﴾ [Yunus: 18], and their saying ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]; and His saying ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, meaning there will be no helper for them just as there is no intercessor. The averting of punishment is either by the intercession of an intercessor or by the help of a helper.

The third: we say: the idafa (annexation) in "kaydihim" is the annexation of the verbal noun to its object, not to its agent. It is as if He said: "the cunning of Satan against them will not avail them." Its explanation is that you say "the striking of Zayd of Amr pleased me" and "the striking of Amr pleased me." If you limit yourself to the verbal noun and its annexed noun, it is known only by context and intention. When you hear someone say "the striking of Zayd pleased me," it may mean that Zayd was the striker, and it may mean that he was the one struck. When you hear someone say "the cutting off of the thief's hand for his theft pleased me," context indicates that it is annexed to the object. If it is said: this is faulty, since it is a clarification of the obvious, for the cunning of one who is plotted against does not benefit in any case, and that is not hidden from anyone, so it needs no explanation; but the cunning of the one who schemes is thought by him to benefit, so the Exalted said: that does not benefit. We say: the cunning of Satan against them regarding the worship of idols, while they thought that they would benefit; and as for their cunning against the Prophet ﷺ, they knew that it would not benefit in the Hereafter, and they only sought that it would benefit them in this world, not in the Hereafter. So the objection turns back against the proponent of the first aspect. There is no objection on both aspects together if you reflect on what we have said.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And indeed, for those who did wrong there is a punishment short of that, but most of them do not know.﴾ There are two views on how this speech connects:

The first: it is connected to His saying ﴿So leave them﴾ [al-Tur: 45], because this indicates the impermissibility of fighting. It has been said that it was revealed before fighting was legislated. In that case it is as if He said: "Leave them, but do not leave them entirely without fighting; rather, for them before the Day of Resurrection there is the punishment of the Day of Badr, when you will be commanded to fight them." So it is an explanation and a promise that abrogates "leave them" with the punishment on the Day of Badr.

The second: it is connected to His saying ﴿will avail nothing﴾. Because when He explained that their scheming would avail them nothing, He said: "Nor does it stop at the non-availing; rather, for them, along with the fact that their scheming avails nothing, there is another woe, namely the punishment prepared for them." Had He said "their scheming will avail them nothing," it would have suggested that it does not benefit them but also does no harm. When He said, "together with that, for those who did wrong there is a punishment," this suggestion was removed. There are issues in this:

The first issue: "those who did wrong" are the people of Makkah if we say the punishment is the punishment of the Day of Badr; if we say the punishment is the punishment of the grave, then "those who did wrong" is general, covering every wrongdoer.

The second issue: What is meant by wrong here? We say there are several views on it:

The first: it is their scheming against their Prophet.

The second: their worship of idols.

The third: their disbelief, and this is suitable to the second view.

The third issue: "short of that" (dūna dhālika), according to the view of most exegetes, means "before" (qabla). This is supported by His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment short of the greater punishment﴾ [al-Sajdah: 21]. It may bear two other meanings:

The first: "short of that" means less than that in duration and severity, as one says, "beating is short of killing in causing pain." Undoubtedly the punishment of this world is less than the punishment of the Hereafter. On this meaning, there is the benefit of alerting to the great punishment of the Hereafter, because when He says "a punishment short of that," meaning killing and punishment in the grave, the reflector thinks: "What is short of killing can only be great." If it is said that this meaning cannot be applied to His saying ﴿the nearer punishment short of the greater punishment﴾, we answer: We grant that, but there is no obstacle to the meaning here being this second one, in the manner of the saying of one who says: "Beneath your obstinacy lie corruptions, and short of your aim lie hardships." Its explanation is that when they worshipped other than God, they wronged themselves by placing themselves in other than the place for which they were created, so it was said to them that for you, short of that wrong, there is a punishment.

The fourth issue: To what does "that" refer? We say the apparent reference is to the Day. There are two other views:

The first: in His saying "they will be struck senseless" and His saying "will avail them" there is a reference to a befalling punishment, so His saying "that" refers to it. It may be said that His saying ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾ [al-Tur: 7] has preceded, and His saying "short of that," meaning short of that punishment.

The second: "short of that" means short of their scheming, so "that" refers to the scheming. We have explained its meaning in the example we gave, which is the saying of one who says: "Beneath your obstinacy is your deprivation." And God knows best.

The fifth issue: ﴿but most of them do not know﴾. We have mentioned several views on it:

The first: it follows the habit of the Arabs, who express the whole by the majority, as God Most High said: ﴿Most of them are believers in Him﴾ [Saba': 41]. Then God spoke in accordance with that custom so that it would be known that God approved of it from the speaker, since in this case it is far from contradiction.

The second: among them were those who believed, so they were not among those who do not know.

The third: they did not know in most circumstances, and in some circumstances they knew; at minimum, they knew at the moment of unveiling, even if it did not benefit them.

The sixth issue: The object of "do not know" may be what preceded of the command, namely that for them there is a punishment short of that; and it may be that it has no object at all, so that the meaning is "most of them are heedless and ignorant."

[Page 237]

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And be patient for the judgment of your Lord, for indeed you are under Our eyes, and glorify your Lord with His praise when you arise﴾. We have mentioned it in our tafsir (exegesis) of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun﴾ [Qaf: 39]. We will point to some of it here, for the lapse of time causes forgetting. So we say: when He, exalted is He, said ﴿So leave them﴾ [al-Tur: 45], it contained an indication that there was no longer any benefit in admonishing them, especially since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if they see a piece of the sky falling﴾ [al-Tur: 44] had preceded. That was among the things that would move the Prophet ﷺ to supplicate, just as Noah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers any dwelling one﴾ [Nuh: 26], and just as Yunus, peace be upon him, supplicated. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And be patient﴾, and replace the curse with glorification: ﴿and glorify your Lord with His praise﴾, instead of your saying, "O Allah, destroy them." Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]?

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿indeed you are under Our eyes﴾, it has several aspects:

The first: when He made clear that they were plotting against him, this, by customary understanding, called for hastening to destroy them, lest their plot be completed. So He said: be patient and do not fear, for you are protected under Our eyes.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: be patient and do not invoke curses upon them, for you are within Our sight; We see you. This state requires that you be in the best of conditions, but your glorifying Us is better than your invoking curses upon servants whom We created. So choose the better, for you are within Our sight.

The third: whoever complains of his state to another indicates that the one complained to does not know the condition of the complainer. So He, exalted is He, said: be patient and do not complain of your state, for you are under Our eyes, and We see you, so there is no benefit in your complaint. Concerning this verse there are issues specific to this place that are not found in His saying ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130].

The first issue: the lam in His saying ﴿for the judgment﴾ (li-hukmi) may carry several meanings:

The first: it has the meaning of "ila" (until), i.e., be patient until Allah judges.

The second: patience here carries the sense of steadfastness, as if He were saying: stand firm for the judgment of your Lord. It is said: "Fulan stood firm (thabata) to bear his opponent" (li-hamli qarnihi).

The third: it is the lam used in the sense of cause. It is said: "Why did you go out?" and one answers: "Because of the ruling of so-and-so upon me to go out." So He said: (be patient), and make the cause of your patience the carrying out of the command, as if He said: be patient for this ruling against you, and not for anything else.

The second issue: here He said ﴿bi-a'yunina﴾ (under Our eyes), while in other places He said ﴿wa-li-tusna'a 'ala 'ayni﴾ (and that you may be made under My eye) [Ta-Ha: 39]. We say: when He used the singular pronoun there, which is the first-person singular ya', He used the singular "eye" ('ayn). When He mentioned here the plural pronoun in His saying "bi-a'yunina", which is the nun of plurality, He used the plural "eyes." This is in terms of wording. As for meaning, the protection here is more complete, because patience is the means to the mercy upon the Prophet ﷺ, since people gathered against him, assembled plots against him, and consulted about his affair. Likewise, He commanded him to build the ark, and commanded him to make the preparation in the absence of water, and protected him from drowning, while all the lands were submerged under water, requiring great protection in the view of the creatures. So He said: "under Our eyes."

The third issue: what is the connection of the ba' (bi) here? We say it has appeared from all the aspects. If we say it is for protection, then its implied sense is "protected under Our eyes." If we say it is for knowledge, its meaning is "within Our sight," i.e., in a place where We see you, and its implied sense is "indeed you are seen by Our eyes." In that case it is like the saying of one who says, "I saw him with my eyes," just as one says, "It was written with the pen," the pen being the instrument, although Allah's seeing is not by an instrument. If it is asked, what is the difference between the two places, where He said in Ta-Ha ﴿under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], and here said "bi-a'yunina," and what is the difference between 'ala and the ba'? We say: the meaning of 'ala there is that he is seen in a manner that Allah is pleased with, as one says: "I will do it under my eye," i.e., according to my approval. Its implied sense is: in a manner that enters into My eye and that I turn to, for whoever does something for another and does not approve of it does not look at it, nor turn his eye toward it.

As for the ba' in His saying ﴿and glorify your Lord with His praise﴾, we have already mentioned it. As for His saying "when you arise" (hina taqum), there are several aspects:

The first: "when you arise" means from your place. What is meant is before rising, at the time you resolve to rise, and at the time of rising. It has been transmitted in a report that "whoever says 'Subhan Allah' before rising from his assembly, that is written for him as an expiation (kaffara)" for what has proceeded from him of words and idle talk in that gathering.

The second: "when you arise from sleep." A report has also been transmitted concerning this indicating that he ﷺ used to "glorify (Allah) after waking."

The third: "when you arise to prayer." It has been transmitted in a report that the Prophet ﷺ used to say at the opening of prayer: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You."

The fourth: "when you arise for some matter," especially when you stand up to strive against your people, oppose them, and invoke curses upon them: ﴿so glorify your Lord with His praise﴾, and exchange your standing for hostility and your rising for vengeance with your standing for the remembrance of Allah and glorifying Him.

The fifth: "when you arise," i.e., during the day, for the night is the place of rest and the day is the place of seeking provision, and rising is more fitting for it. This is like His saying ﴿and during the night, glorify Him﴾ [Qaf: 40], an indication to what remains of time. Likewise ﴿and at the retreat of the stars﴾ [Qaf: 40], which is the beginning of dawn.

And as for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And during part of the night, glorify Him, and at the retreat of the stars﴾.

Its interpretation has already been given, and it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [Ar-Rum: 17]. We have already mentioned the benefit of singling out these times and its meaning. We will close this surah with a benefit: He, Exalted is He, said here ﴿and at the retreat of the stars﴾, and He said in Qaf ﴿and after the prostrations﴾ [Qaf: 40]. It may be said that the meaning is one and the same, and that what is meant by "prostrations" is the plural of "sajid" (one who prostrates), and the stars also have prostration, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 6]. It has also been said that what is meant by "najm" (star) is the stars of the sky. It has been said that "najm" is what has no stem among plants, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [An-Nahl: 49]. Or what is meant by "the stars" is the prescribed duties (wazifah), and every prescribed duty is called a "najm" in the language, meaning: when you finish the duties of the prayer, then say "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah). It has indeed been reported in a hadith: "Whoever says after the prayer, 'Subhan Allah' ten times, 'Al-hamdu lillah' ten times, and 'Allahu Akbar' ten times, a thousand good deeds will be written for him." So the meaning in both places is one, because prostration is among the prescribed duties. The well-known and apparent view is that what is meant by "the retreat of the stars" is the time of dawn, when the star turns away, becomes hidden, and its light disappears with the light of the sun. At that point, what we mentioned as the fifth aspect in His saying "when you arise" becomes clear: that what is meant by it is the daytime, because it is the place of standing up. ("And during part of the night") refers to the portion during which a person is awake, ﴿and at the retreat of the stars﴾ refers to the time of dawn, so one is never excused from glorifying Him except during the time of sleep. This is the end of the interpretation of this surah, and Allah knows best. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad (ﷺ), his family, and grant them peace.
